$comment: Scope: the external "brick" linear power supply, the mainboard RF modulator, and the mains side. Everything below each root is inline. Shared upstream ids are referenced by string. Note that 120407 is the PSU assembly number; 250407 is the C64 motherboard assembly number - they are not the same thing (see the note on c64.psu).

roots.name: Commodore 64 external 'brick' power supply
roots.description: A sealed black ABS box roughly 150 x 100 x 60 mm that sits under the C64 and converts wall mains into 5 V DC for the logic plus unfiltered ~9 V AC for the cassette motor, the RF modulator, the VIC-II's CAN +5 V rail, the SID's +12 V doubler and the 50/60 Hz time-of-day clock. It is a linear supply: an iron-core transformer, two rectifier diodes, one 4700 uF electrolytic, one three-terminal 5 V regulator and a folded aluminium heatsink, all buried under a minty-green epoxy pour from 1983 on.

facts.label: Input
facts.value: 117 V 50/60 Hz, 40-46 VA (North American 902503-02 / 251053-02 builds)

facts.label: 5 V DC output
facts.value: 7.5-8.5 W rated (1.5-1.7 A), unregulated 5 V AC rail separate

facts.label: 9 V AC output
facts.value: 6.7-9.0 VA, unfiltered sine, galvanically separate winding

facts.label: Output connector
facts.value: 6-pin round DIN (4-pin on some builds)

facts.label: Approvals seen on case
facts.value: UL 13J5 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER', CSA, NLS, 'SHOCK HAZARD DO NOT OPEN'

facts.label: Made in
facts.value: Singapore (251053-02); transformer marked 'MP' (Miles-Platts, UK)

roots.note: Part-number correction: the external supply is ASSY 120407; 250407 is the C64 *motherboard* (the version in this tree's spine file). Regulator silicon changed three times in three years: a discrete 2N3055/2N3792 pass transistor in the earliest 'repairable' silver-label boxes, a plain 7805-class three-pin regulator in the potted 1983-84 units, and a Sanken SI-3052P in the later 902503-02. Diodes are 400GI or 1N5400, not 1N4001, in most builds. No common-mode choke and no zinc-oxide varistor belong here: two fully inventoried depotted 251053-02 builds (3-83 and 13-83) list every component (diodes, regulator, two resistors, tantalums, fuse, transformer) with neither part present, so the previous contains edges were removed rather than left as speculation.

children.name: Mains transformer, 40-46 VA
children.description: The whole of the supply's energy conversion. One primary on 117 V mains, a centre-tapped ~18 V secondary feeding the 5 V regulator, and a separate ~9 V winding feeding straight out to the C64. The two secondaries are galvanically isolated from each other as well as from the primary - that isolation is what lets the C64 tie their grounds together only at the rectifier. Every wound transformer is proved before it is potted or assembled: a 1500-2500 V AC dielectric withstand between primary and all secondaries, an insulation-resistance check at 500 V DC, a turns-ratio and phasing check between the taps, and a loaded run at nominal line voltage.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 40 VA (3-83 build) / 46 W (13-83 build) input at 117 V 60 Hz

facts.label: 9 V winding
facts.value: 9 V AC 9.0 VA, protected by a 3 A fuse in the conductor

facts.label: HV winding
facts.value: 18 V AC centre-tapped, pins 6/7/8 on 902503-02, protected by a 5 A (slow) fuse

facts.label: Maker's mark
facts.value: MP (Miles-Platts, Leicester, UK - bobbins and insulation systems)

facts.label: Dielectric withstand before potting
facts.value: 1500-2500 V AC for 1 s between primary and all secondaries, per UL 478 / IEC 65 practice for unlisted components

facts.label: Insulation resistance
facts.value: >=2 MOhm at 500 V DC

facts.label: Ratio and phasing check
facts.value: secondary voltage within +/-5% of nominal at rated load, and the taps in phase

facts.label: Loaded run
facts.value: at nominal line voltage, checking regulation and temperature rise

children.note: The 'MP' mark on the core is most likely Miles-Platts (founded 1971, a UK bobbin and insulation specialist whose own company history lists inch-lamination and metric-lamination bobbins), i.e. the coil former and interwinding materials rather than necessarily the whole assembly.

children.name: E-I laminated silicon-steel core
children.description: A stack of punched E and I laminations with interleaved joints, taped along the yoke edges with a single wrap of masking or Kapton tape. For a 40 VA unit at 60 Hz the stack is maybe 25-35 mm tall in 0.35-0.5 mm plate, and it is clamped hard enough that the laminations must be isolated from each other by the oxide scale left on the punched edges.

facts.label: Lamination thickness
facts.value: 0.35 mm or 0.5 mm electrical sheet (era range for small power transformers)

facts.label: Material
facts.value: grain-oriented electrical steel, silicon content ~2-3.5 wt%

facts.label: Lamination pitch
facts.value: roughly 20-30 mm; E and I interleaved in a 2:1 or 3:2 sequence

children.note: This brick is a laminated-steel design, not a ferrite design: the 251053-02 teardown shows a stack of discrete plates taped along the yoke edges, not a moulded core. Ferrite E/U or E/I cores do appear in later Commodore supplies (the C64C and C16/Plus4 white bricks), where a moulded MnZn core gave a smaller, lighter, lower-loss assembly at several times the material cost and a supply chain in Japan or Germany rather than the local steel mill; that alternative is set out at c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative, whose powder metallurgy is the shared metal.ferrite line.

children.name: MnZn ferrite E-core alternative
children.description: Later Commodore bricks and the C64C/Plus4 supplies switched to a pressed manganese-zinc ferrite core. Ferrite has much higher resistivity than silicon steel so it can be used as a solid moulded shape with no lamination joints, giving lower core loss at 60 Hz and a much lighter assembly - at several times the material cost, and with a supply chain in Japan or Germany rather than the local steel mill.

facts.label: Resistivity
facts.value: ~10^5 ohm.m vs ~5x10^-7 ohm.m for silicon steel

facts.label: Saturation
facts.value: ~0.4-0.5 T (much lower than steel, so the core must be bigger)

facts.label: Loss at 50-60 Hz
facts.value: 5-20 kW/m3 at 200 mT

facts.label: Blend
facts.value: Fe2O3 50-60 mol%, MnO 5-15 mol%, ZnO 15-30 mol%, ball-milled 24-48 h to 1-5 um

facts.label: Bind and fire
facts.value: 1-3% PVA binder plus a stearate lubricant, green density ~3.0-3.3 g/cm3, fired at 1100-1250 C for 1-6 h in air or oxygen, 12-18% linear shrinkage

children.note: Not the design in this brick: the 251053-02 teardown is plainly a stack of punched steel laminations. The alternative belongs to later Commodore supplies and is set out here because the comparison is the whole point of the choice - about 10^5 ohm.m against roughly 5x10^-7 ohm.m for silicon steel, at half to a third the saturation induction, so the ferrite core must be physically larger even though it is lighter. Which Commodore part numbers used ferrite could not be verified per part number from a primary source; mark the supply chain as unconfirmed. The oxide blend, the pressing and the firing are the shared metal.ferrite line.

children.name: Enamelled copper winding
children.description: The primary, the 18 V centre-tapped secondary and the 9 V output secondary are wound in layers on a moulded bobbin, with a few hundred turns of 0.25-0.4 mm enamelled copper wire. Layer insulation between each pass and interleaved padding between the primary and the secondaries carry the 1000-1500 V RMS of the mains.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.25-0.4 mm enamelled copper, roughly 500-1200 turns per winding

facts.label: Insulation class
facts.value: class H, 180 C, by virtue of the enamel

facts.label: Layout
facts.value: layer winding; primary nearest the bobbin or outermost, secondaries separated

children.name: Enamelled magnet wire
children.description: Bare copper rod drawn down to 0.25-0.4 mm through a series of tungsten-carbide or diamond dies, then coated in two or more passes of a thermosetting enamel - typically polyester-imide (Grade 2 / THEIC) - and baked to cure it. Each coat adds roughly 5-10 um, so a double-grade wire has 25-40% more copper per given window area than bare wire.

facts.label: Wire diameter
facts.value: 0.25-0.4 mm bare, 0.28-0.45 mm with enamel

facts.label: Enamel
facts.value: polyester-imide, 2 coats, ~35-45 um total build

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 160-200 C oven, 5-10 h depending on line speed

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: Grade 2 = ~2x the diameter in insulation for the same wire

facts.label: Copper feedstock
facts.value: blister copper from concentrate of 20-40 wt% Cu, milled from porphyry ore of 0.4-1.0 wt% Cu ground to about 100 um for flotation

children.name: Moulded nylon bobbin
children.description: A spool-shaped coil former in glass-filled or unfilled nylon 6 or nylon 6,6, with cheek flanges that locate it on the core leg and a continuous slot that keeps the layer insulation in place. Bobbins were (and still are) a Miles-Platts product line, which fits the 'MP' mark found on this transformer.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: nylon 6 or nylon 6,6, sometimes 30% glass filled

facts.label: Process
facts.value: injection moulding, 2.5-5 mm wall

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: nylon 6 from caprolactam by the Beckmann rearrangement of cyclohexanone, itself from catalytic air oxidation of cyclohexane, which comes from benzene hydrogenation

children.name: Interwinding earth screen
children.description: The protective-earth conductor is bonded to an aluminium or copper foil laid between the primary and the secondary windings - or sometimes to the transformer frame bolt. It does not leave the transformer: the earthing path is closed inside the potted block and never reaches the plastic case or the computer. The foil is plain rolled aluminium or copper, lapped and left uncut so it cannot tear, and it is deliberately insulated from both windings.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: aluminium or copper foil, 0.02-0.05 mm, lapped to a tab

facts.label: Termination
facts.value: crimp ring or soldered to the earth conductor of the line cord

children.note: Observed on the 902503-02: the protective-earth pin 'somehow connects to the transformer, looks like it goes in the layer between the primary and secondary winding', and does not extend to the output. The brick is all-plastic, so there is nothing to bond earth to on the outside.

Not established: the 0.25-0.4 mm wire, the 500-1200 turns per winding, the 18 V centre-tapped and 9 V secondaries, the layer layout, and the class H 180 C rating by virtue of the enamel. The 902503-02 teardown confirms the winding structure - 9 V AC on pins 9 and 11, and "18V AC with a 'center' tab on pin 6" - but no source documents the wire gauge, turn count or insulation class for this transformer.

children.name: Transformer pin terminal board
children.description: A row of brass pins on a small phenolic or nylon board carrying the primary, the interwinding earth, and all the secondary taps. The rectifier diodes and fuses in the 1983-84 bricks are soldered straight onto these pins, which is why the schematic 'terminals' that appear in a teardown are the transformer's own pins rather than a separate board.

facts.label: Pins
facts.value: 8-12 brass pins on 2.54 mm pitch

facts.label: Board material
facts.value: phenolic (paper/phenol formaldehyde) or nylon

facts.label: 902503-02 numbering
facts.value: pins 6/7/8 = centre-tapped 18 V; pins 9/11 = 9 V AC; 10 and 12 = unused spares

children.name: Rectifier diodes, 400GI / 1N5400
children.description: Two or four stud-less axial rectifier diodes convert the 18 V centre-tapped secondary into pulsating DC. The 902503-02 uses two General Electric 400GI silicon rectifiers in a full-wave centre-tapped configuration, which saves the two extra dice of a bridge; other builds use four 1N5400s or a moulded bridge. The diodes are soldered directly onto the transformer pins.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: GE 400GI (as marked on the 902503-02) or 1N5400, 3 A class

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: full-wave centre-tapped (2 diodes) on the 902503-02; some builds use a 4-diode bridge

facts.label: Vf at 1 A
facts.value: ~0.9-1.1 V for a 1N5400; the 400GI is noticeably slower and hotter

children.note: The 400GI is a slow-recovery rectifier with a large forward drop for its rating; hobbyists have observed it running well outside its current specification, and it is a recurring failure item. The correct part for the job is a 1N5400.

children.name: Axial rectifier diode
children.description: A single silicon junction in an axial package with a formed lead, cathode band marked with a stripe. Inside: a die a few hundred microns across with a heavy anode metallisation, a glass passivation, and epoxy or a voidless glass body filled with silicone stress-relief gel to survive the power cycling.

facts.label: Vceo / Vrrm
facts.value: 50-100 V reverse for a 400GI; 100 V for 1N5400

facts.label: If (av)
facts.value: 3 A at 75 C lead temperature for a 1N5400

facts.label: Body
facts.value: epoxy-filled axial (DO-201AD) or glass-butt

children.name: Silicon rectifier die
children.description: A 100-150 mm wafer ground to a die typically 2 x 2 x 0.3 mm, with a diffused N-type cathode and metallised anode. The same Czochralski silicon as the VIC-II and the 6510; the detailed wafer process belongs to the silicon branch of this tree.

facts.label: Junction depth
facts.value: ~20-40 um phosphorus diffusion

facts.label: Die
facts.value: ~2 x 2 mm after dicing

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO at 1800-2000 C, 97-99% metallurgical grade

facts.label: Upgraded grade
facts.value: 9-11N (99.9999999%) before the single crystal is pulled

facts.label: Feedstock
facts.value: high-purity quartz lump and petroleum coke

children.name: Moulded bridge rectifier alternative
children.description: Some builds and most replacement supplies use a packaged bridge: four dice mounted on a common ceramic or moulded body with the terminals formed into the four corners. Commodore's own choice of two discrete diodes over a bridge saved two dice and one package, at the cost of a centre tap on the transformer.

facts.label: Bridge
facts.value: e.g. Varo VMO8, listed in the C64 service manual parts list as CR4 with Commodore stock number 906129-01

children.note: Not established: the 1N5400's ratings as quoted (100 V reverse, 3 A average at 75 C lead temperature), the DO-201AD epoxy-filled axial body, and the practice of marking the cathode with a stripe for the parts used in this supply. The 902503-02 teardown records only that the rectifier diodes "should be marked 1N5400"; no datasheet-level source was consulted.

children.name: 5 V linear voltage regulator
children.description: The pass element that turns roughly 8-10 V of pulsating DC into 5.00 V. Three different implementations appear in C64 bricks inside two years, and the choice of which one determines how much heat has to be removed. At full load the drop across the pass device is 3-5 V at 1.5 A, so 4.5-7.5 W has to go into the heatsink - which is why these supplies run hot and why the electrolytics above them cook.

facts.label: Dissipation
facts.value: ~3 W at 8 V in / 1 A out; ~8 W at 10.4 V in / 1.4 A out

facts.label: Efficiency
facts.value: ~40-50% for the whole brick, dominated by the series pass

children.note: The failure mode that destroyed C64s is the pass device shorting the input to the output, putting ~8-10 V on a rail designed for 5 V. Unloaded 5.3 V is normal; 5.4 V is the number to worry about; below 4.6 V the machine will not boot.

children.name: 7805-class three-pin regulator
children.description: The simplest form: a monolithic regulator containing the reference, error amplifier, current limit and the pass transistor, in a TO-220 or TO-3P-like plastic body with a tab bolted to the heatsink. In the 251053-02 brick it is a three-legged part with rectangular legs, screwed straight into the folded aluminium plate under a blob of epoxy.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 V, 1.5 A continuous for a 7805 in a TO-220 with a small copper tab

facts.label: Current limit
facts.value: internally ~2.2 A thermal-limited foldback

facts.label: Mounting
facts.value: single bolt through the tab into the heatsink plate

children.name: Sanken SI-3052P integrated regulator
children.description: The regulator in the later 902503-02, which many hobbyists misidentify as a transistor because it is moulded in a TO-3P-looking package. It is a 5 V / 2 A linear regulator with an internal error amplifier and a foldback current limit that kicks in at about 2.4 A. The datasheet explicitly warns that the output must not be raised by inserting a resistor in the ground pin - and Commodore inserted a 300 Ohm resistor in the ground pin anyway, to make up for the drop in the output cable.

facts.label: Maker
facts.value: Sanken Electric (the 'SK' in the part number is Sanken's logo)

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 V fixed, 2 A

facts.label: Current limit
facts.value: ~2.4 A foldback

facts.label: Ground-lift resistor
facts.value: 300 Ohm nominal (some builds 30 Ohm) from the regulator ground pin to the output return

children.note: The ground-lift trick raises the output a few tens of millivolts to compensate for the resistive drop of a metre of thin output wire, but it also corrupts the regulator's ground reference and interferes with its current-limit behaviour - the datasheet says so in Note 3. Modifying this circuit is the standard modern replacement and is well documented.

children.name: Output stability capacitor
children.description: A small electrolytic or tantalum directly across the regulator's input and output pins. The datasheet requires it for loop stability; a 2.2 uF 16 V tantalum appears on some 902503-02 builds and the 3-83 version has the holes for it but does not populate it, which suggests it was a late cost change.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: 2.2 uF 16 V tantalum (populated on some builds, holes only on others)

children.name: Discrete 2N3055 / 2N3792 series-pass regulator
children.description: The earliest 'repairable' silver-label brick used a discrete design: an NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can bolted to a heatsink as the series pass, a smaller driver transistor, a zener or low-current regulator as the reference, wirewound resistors in the emitter and base for current limiting, and a thermal shutdown in contact with the heatsink. It is the arrangement the 902503-02's monolithic regulator replaced.

facts.label: Pass transistor
facts.value: 2N3055 (15 A / 60 V, TO-3) or 2N3792 (1.5 A class NPN, TO-3)

facts.label: Vbe multiplier error amp
facts.value: two-transistor error amplifier sensing the output through a divider

facts.label: Emitter ballast
facts.value: wirewound resistor to force a minimum standing current and to limit current sharing

children.note: No verified transcription of the 120407 discrete-regulator schematic is available (lemon64's forum is behind a bot challenge). The topology and part families described here are the standard 1982 discrete 5 V linear supply of this size; the exact part numbers are unconfirmed for this specific assembly.

children.name: 2N3055 / 2N3792 power NPN
children.description: A triple-diffused planar NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can: a bolted metal header with an isolation disc, the die brazed or soldered to the header, one or two emitter bonds, and a hermetic can with a glass-sealed pin feedthrough. The 2N3055 is grossly oversized for a 1.5 A load (15 A, 60 V, 115 W dissipation capability), which is exactly why it was chosen: it could not fail thermally even when the circuit was badly designed.

facts.label: 2N3055
facts.value: NPN, 15 A Ic, 60 V Vceo, Pc 115 W with a good heat sink

facts.label: 2N3792
facts.value: NPN power transistor, roughly 1.5 A / 60 V class, TO-3

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: triple-diffused planar (collector-base, base-emitter, collector-emitter diffusions)

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-3 can, 40-60 g of nickel-plated copper, mica or thin mica-fibre washer under the can

children.note: Modern practice for a 1.5 A rail is an 8-20 A TO-220 or a DPAK/LDO with an active current limit; the 2N3055 in a TO-3 is expensive and a thermal mismatch, but it was the safest thing an engineer could buy off the shelf in 1982.

children.name: Driver / error-amplifier transistor
children.description: A small-signal NPN whose job is to supply the ~0.7 V of base drive plus the feedback signal the pass transistor needs. In a 1982 discrete supply this is typically a TO-92 part with hFE around 100-400, or one half of a matched pair. Its collector dissipation is small but its junction temperature is close to the pass transistor's, so it shares the same heatsink metal.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: TO-92 small-signal NPN, e.g. 2N3904 / BC547 class

facts.label: Base drive
facts.value: ~0.6-0.8 V above the pass emitter, set by the Vbe multiplier

children.note: The C64 mainboard itself uses 2N3904 and 2N4401 in TO-92 packages for its audio and cassette motor drives (Q1-Q8 in the 326298 parts list), so the same parts bins would have supplied the brick.

children.name: Voltage reference
children.description: In a 1982 discrete supply the reference is either a 5.1-6.2 V zener diode biased from a constant-current source, or a low-current three-terminal regulator such as a TL431 or a small 7805 in a TO-92 used purely as a reference. The zener route needs a stable bias current; the temperature coefficient of an ordinary zener is poor, which shows up as output drift with case temperature.

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: ~0.1%/C for an uncompensated zener vs ~0.005%/C for a bandgap reference

children.note: Modern practice is a bandgap reference inside the regulator IC, giving ±0.5% over temperature; the zener plus Vbe-multiplier arrangement of 1982 gave ±3-5% and drifted with case temperature.

children.name: Emitter ballast resistors
children.description: One to three wirewound resistors in series with the pass transistor's emitter. Their purpose is to develop a signal proportional to output current for current limiting and to force a standing current through the pass transistor so its hFE and therefore the loop gain do not collapse at light load. Wirewound rather than film because the dissipation is fractional watts but the temperature rise has to stay small.

facts.label: Values
facts.value: 0.1-1 Ohm, 1-3 W wirewound, manganin or constantan

facts.label: Temperature coefficient
facts.value: chosen near zero for manganin, positive for constantan

children.note: Ballast resistors were largely abandoned in integrated regulators because the current-limit loop senses the emitter directly through a pin.

children.name: Manganin wire
children.description: A copper-manganese-nickel alloy (typically 86% Cu, 12% Mn, 2% Ni) whose resistivity barely changes with temperature. A spiral-wound wirewound resistor is made by winding manganin or constantan wire onto a ceramic or plastic former and baking it under high tension so the winding stress-relaxes and stays against the form.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: ~86 Cu / 12 Mn / 2 Ni (manganin) or ~60 Cu / 40 Ni (constantan)

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: <10 ppm/K for manganin

children.name: Thermal shutdown
children.description: A temperature-sensitive element in contact with the heatsink - a thermistor or a bimetallic thermal switch - that shorts or removes the driver bias when the sink passes roughly 90-110 C, so the supply folds back rather than destroying itself. Commodore's bricks more often relied on a thermal fuse in the primary and on the epoxy pot for heat retention, which is the root of their reputation.

facts.label: Trip temperature
facts.value: ~95-110 C typical for a thermal switch

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: bimetal opens a contact, or an SCR crowbar latches a short

children.note: The 251053-02 teardowns document a thermal fuse in series with the primary winding, but no thermal shutdown switch inside the regulator board is documented.

children.name: NTC thermistor
children.description: A bead or disc of semiconducting metal oxide whose resistance falls steeply with temperature (10 kOhm at 25 C, ~1 kOhm at 100 C for the standard 10K curve). Glued or bolted to the heatsink and shunting the driver bias, it gives a soft, non-resetting protection that must cool before it re-conducts.

facts.label: Resistance
facts.value: 10 kOhm at 25 C, B = 3435 K curve

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ferric oxide or manganese oxide semiconducting ceramic

children.name: Folded aluminium heatsink
children.description: A thin aluminium plate folded into a U so that one leg clamps under the case and the other presents an area against the regulator. There are no fins: the design relies on the natural convection of a brick sitting under a desk. It is the reason the case runs at 60-70 C and the epoxy never fully cools. The sheet is commercial-purity aluminium folded on a press brake and tapped for the regulator screw, usually left mill finish or painted, occasionally black anodised.

facts.label: Geometry
facts.value: flat sheet folded into a U, ~1-2 mm thick, no fins

facts.label: Dissipation
facts.value: 3-8 W at a 35-45 C rise above ambient

facts.label: Surface finish
facts.value: mill finish, painted, or black anodised (sulphuric acid bath at 20 C, 1-2 V at 0.5-1 A/dm2, 5-25 um film sealed in boiling water); on a folded sheet with no fins the emissivity gain is marginal

facts.label: Stock
facts.value: commercial-purity aluminium sheet, 1050 or 3003 and 99.0-99.7% Al, off a rolling ingot from a Hall-Heroult pot running at 950-970 C in molten cryolite on roughly 13,000-15,000 kWh per tonne

children.note: Modern practice would use an extruded finned profile in 6063 aluminium; a folded sheet U gives only 0.02-0.04 m2 of surface, an order of magnitude less than the fins a switching supply would use for the same power.

children.name: 4700 uF 16 V aluminium electrolytic
children.description: The single reservoir capacitor on the rectifier output. It is the part that has killed the most C64s: as the electrolyte dries out the ripple current is no longer smoothed, the series regulator loses headroom and starts pumping 100/120 Hz ripple onto the 5 V rail, and eventually the cap leaks current into the regulator's ground reference and pushes the output up past 5.5 V. Replacements are still sold as the C64 'fix' four decades later.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: 4700 uF / 16 V radial (2200 uF in some builds; 2200 uF / 16 V on the C64 mainboard itself)

facts.label: Lifetime
facts.value: rated 2000 h at 85 C; real service life 10-20 years at 40 C ambient

children.note: Two capacitors in parallel have lower ESR than either alone, which is why both the replacement-PSU literature and the datasheets push for two. Failure is not dramatic: capacitance drifts down, ESR climbs, ripple appears, and eventually the leakage current rises far enough to upset the regulator.

children.name: Tantalum and small electrolytic capacitors
children.description: Secondary filtering: a 0.22 uF 35 V tantalum and a 47 uF 10 V electrolytic on the 5 V output for stability and for the load transients the VIC-II produces when it banks memory. The tantalum is polar and fails short, so it is the more dramatic failure of the pair.

facts.label: Tantalum
facts.value: 0.22 uF / 35 V, epoxy-dipped bead or drop

facts.label: Electrolytic
facts.value: 47 uF / 10 V radial

facts.label: Resistors
facts.value: 100 Ohm and 22 Ohm carbon-film, embedded in the epoxy pour

children.name: Small regulator PCB, 'PNE-5'
children.description: A single-sided glass-epoxy board about 40 x 30 mm carrying the regulator, the two electrolytics, the tantalum and two resistors, with the identification 'PNE-5' etched into the copper on the earlier build and no marking at all on the later one. It is held in place only by the epoxy that floods the whole case, which is why de-potting usually breaks it.

facts.label: Marking
facts.value: 'PNE-5' etched into the copper on the 3-83 build; unmarked on the 13-83

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: FR-4 glass-epoxy, ~1.6 mm, single sided

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: single-sided, no plated-through holes, tracks and pads in 35 um copper

facts.label: Substrate detail
facts.value: FR-4 glass-epoxy, Tg ~135-150 C at the usual ~18-20% resin loading, UL 94 V-0; prepreg and foil pressed at 160-200 C and 1-3 MPa for 30-60 min

children.name: Black ABS enclosure
children.description: A two-half injection-moulded case in black ABS, ~150 x 100 x 60 mm, with a tongue-and-groove seam, ribbing on the sides for stiffness, four case screws and one larger screw holding the cable clamp. On the potted builds the seam is a line of epoxy. Some units have the rating text moulded into the plastic; others have it printed on the underside and on a metallised label.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene), natural or black

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB is the normal requirement for a PSU enclosure; V-2 or V-0 is required if it is a subassembly of a listed appliance

facts.label: Markings
facts.value: moulded into the casing on the 3-83 build; printed on the underside with a metalised date sticker on the 13-83

facts.label: UL 94 HB
facts.value: burning rate <= 1 mm/s over the first 100 mm on a 125 x 13 x 13 mm bar conditioned 48 h at 23 C / 50% RH

facts.label: UL 94 V-0
facts.value: flame out within 10 s and no glowing after 30 s, no drips

children.note: ABS is used because it is tough, chemically inert to the epoxy and the PVC of the cord, and injection moulds to a good surface for the moulded-in lettering. It burns readily - which is why the flammability rating and the 94-HB test are part of the approval, not decoration.

children.name: Case screws
children.description: Cross-recessed pan-head self-tapping screws into moulded bosses in the plastic, and in a mains appliance they must be short enough that they cannot reach the primary wiring - a specific check in the safety audit.

facts.label: Fastener
facts.value: 3.5 x 10 mm pan-head cross recess, zinc-plated steel

facts.label: Safety rule
facts.value: no screw long enough to contact a live part

children.note: Not established: the 3.5 x 10 mm pan-head cross-recess zinc-plated fastener, or the specific safety rule that no screw may be long enough to reach a live part. Screw geometry and plating are common practice but no source consulted states either the size or the rule for this case.

children.name: 6-pin DIN output connector
children.description: A moulded round DIN socket on the case face carrying the two 5 V conductors, the two 9 V AC conductors and, in the six-pin version, the second 9 V AC leg. Later builds reduced it to four pins. The C64's mainboard has the mating plug, and the two ends of the 5 V pair are deliberately larger-diameter so the plug cannot be inserted backwards.

facts.label: Pins
facts.value: 6 on the 120407-era and 251053-02 builds; 4 on some later revisions

facts.label: Assignment (902503-02)
facts.value: pin 2 = 0 V return, pin 5 = +5 V, pins 6 and 7 = the two 9 V AC legs

facts.label: Housing
facts.value: nylon or phenolic shell over brass pins

children.note: The 902503-02 schematic labels the output as 5 V DC 7.5A; 7.5 W (1.5 A) is the correct figure and the 'A' is a long-standing typo on Commodore's own drawing.

children.name: Connector nylon shell and brass pins
children.description: The shell is moulded from a glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF) with a chamfered keyway that defines the pin polarisation; the pins are brass, often nickel-plated for wear, and are a press-fit or riveted into the shell. The 5 V pins are larger so that the plug is keyed by power, not by numbering.

facts.label: Shell material
facts.value: PA66-GF30 or phenolic, UL 94 V-0

facts.label: Pins
facts.value: brass, 0.8-1.0 mm, nickel-plated

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: circular DIN, 180 degrees between pins

children.note: Not established: PA66-GF30 or phenolic at UL 94 V-0, brass pins 0.8-1.0 mm nickel-plated, the chamfered keyway, or the 180 degree circular DIN pitch. The 1992 service manual identifies the machine-side connector as CN7 and gives its pin functions, but the moulded shell, its glass-filled nylon and its keying are not documented in any source consulted.

children.name: Power indicator LED
children.description: Not present on every brick. Where fitted it is a 3 mm red LED in a small nylon bezel, fed from the 5 V rail through a 330 Ohm to 1 kOhm resistor so that the constant ~7 mA is well inside the LED's safe operating current, and the resistor - not the LED - is what limits the current when the rail is at 5.4 V.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: 3 mm diffused red LED, ~1.6-2.0 V forward drop

facts.label: Series resistor
facts.value: 330 Ohm - 1 kOhm carbon film

children.note: Confirmed only on some replacement bricks; not verified inside an original Commodore brick, and the 251053-02 teardown photo descriptions do not mention one. The 3-83/13-83 case markings list only 'power supply', no indicator, which suggests the indicator is on later units only.

children.name: Rating label and moulded markings
children.description: The safety-critical data: input volts and frequency, VA input, 5 V DC watts, 9 V AC VA, the approval marks and the warning text. On the 3-83 build the text is moulded into the case; on the 13-83 it is printed on the underside, duplicated on a top label and given a date on a metallised sticker. Every approval scheme requires this data to be legible without opening the unit.

facts.label: 3-83 build
facts.value: 117 V 50/60 Hz 40 VA in; 5 V DC 7.5 W and 9 V AC 6.7 VA out; UL 13J5; 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER'

facts.label: 13-83 build
facts.value: 117 V 50/60 Hz 46 W in; 5 V DC 8.5 W and 9 V AC 9 VA out; CSA and NLS marks; 'SHOCK HAZARD DO NOT OPEN' in English and French

children.name: Metallised polyester label
children.description: A 25 um metallised polyester film printed with one or two hit spot colours and applied with an acrylic adhesive. Metallised polyester is used because it is tear-resistant, solvent-resistant and survives the polyester solvents in the potting epoxy, unlike paper.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: 25 um metallised BOPP or polyester

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: acrylic, applied by pressure-sensitive transfer

children.note: Not established: that the rating label on this supply is a 25 um metallised polyester film with a pressure-sensitive acrylic adhesive, that it is printed in one or two spot colours, or that paper was excluded because it does not survive the potting epoxy's solvents. Metallised BOPP and vacuum-deposited aluminium are documented as such, but no source describes a mains rating label.

children.name: Rocker switch
children.description: A mains switch in the line conductor, mounted in the case wall so the rocker is the only part exposed. It is a snap-action mechanism: a spring-loaded plunger forces a moving contact against a fixed one with a definite wiping motion as it passes through centre, which both makes the circuit and scrapes oxide off the contact faces.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: ~6 A at 250 V AC for a small rocker

facts.label: Contact alloy
facts.value: silver or a silver-nickel brazed contact on a brass carrier

facts.label: Endurance
facts.value: ~10,000 operations typical for a 1980s rocker

children.note: Not established for the brick's own switch: its rating, contact alloy, endurance figure, or the snap-action wiping mechanism. The C64's own supply switch is a documented, numbered part - the 1992 service manual parts list gives SW1 as "Rocker Switch DPDT 904500-01" on the connector panel "(Power, ON, OFF) 251095-01", and the circuit theory states that the filtered 5 V rail "is then controlled by on/off switch S1" - but that is the machine's switch, not the brick's, and the double-pole configuration corroborates only the note that the machine's switch interrupts both supplies.

children.name: Silver-alloy contacts and arc erosion
children.description: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of any metal and, unlike copper, its oxide is still conductive, so a silver contact keeps working even when it blackens. Contacts are riveted or welded to brass carriers so the spring force is set by the carrier rather than by the contact material. Every make operation evaporates a microscopic amount of metal as an arc; the contact is sized so that tens of thousands of makes erode it only slightly, and so that a failed contact fails open rather than welded shut.

facts.label: Contact material
facts.value: Ag, Ag-SnO2 or Ag-Ni, on a brass or phosphor-bronze carrier

facts.label: Contact force
facts.value: ~1-3 N, giving a low and stable contact resistance

facts.label: Erosion rate
facts.value: ~0.01-0.1 mm per 10,000 operations in the worst case

children.note: Not established, and partly contradicted: the reason given for preferring silver - that its oxide is still electrically conductive. The conductivity ranking is documented ("The electrical conductivity of silver is the highest of all metals, greater even than copper") and silver's blackening is documented ("silver tarnishes in air to form the black silver sulfide"), but the silver article describes an amphoteric oxide, not a conducting one, so the load-bearing claim is unsupported. Also unestablished: Ag-SnO2 contact practice in 1980s mains switches, the ~1-3 N contact force and the erosion rate.

children.name: Rocker actuator and case
children.description: The external rocker is moulded in a glass-filled thermoset or a self-extinguishing thermoplastic and clips over a phenolic or nylon body carrying the fixed contacts. The case must be rated for the insulation class and have the flammability rating appropriate to an appliance, and the actuator must not be able to be jammed in the on position.

facts.label: Case material
facts.value: phenolic or nylon 66, UL 94 V-0

facts.label: Creepage
facts.value: ~4 mm between line and neutral terminals, set by the moulding

children.note: Not established: the UL 94 V-0 rating, the nylon 66 or phenolic case material, or the ~4 mm creepage between line and neutral terminals. Nylon 66 and glass-reinforced grades of it are documented as injection-moulded and as capable of being made fire retardant, but no source ties those facts to a mains switch actuator or gives the creepage figure.

children.name: Primary fuse and thermal fuse
children.description: Two serial protections on the mains side. The primary fuse is a small cartridge type rated at roughly 120 mA (115 V) or 200 mA (230 V), sized at about 125% of the running input current so the transformer draws its inrush without nuisance failure. The second, documented in the 251053-02, is a thermal fuse in series with one end of the primary: a fusible alloy element that opens irreversibly if the transformer overheats.

facts.label: Primary fuse rating
facts.value: reported 120 mA / 200 mA, depending on build and mains voltage

facts.label: Secondary fuses
facts.value: 3 A in the 9 V AC conductor, 5 A slow-blow in the rectifier conductor of the 902503-02

facts.label: Thermal fuse
facts.value: in series with one end of the primary winding on the 251053-02

children.note: The 3 A fuse in the 9 V AC conductor exists so a short on the output cable cannot damage the transformer before the brick is ever plugged into a C64; the 5 A slow fuse in the rectifier conductor is sized for the charging surge of the 4700 uF reservoir capacitor. Build variation, documented: the 3-83 teardown shows a 5 A 250 V fuse in-line with the 9 V AC output (glass body, visible poking out of the epoxy) and no 2.2 uF tantalum (holes present but unpopulated), while the 13-83 has the tantalum; the 3 A versus 5 A 9 V-conductor ratings differ by build and source and are not reconciled.

children.name: Glass cartridge fuse
children.description: A fuse element of pure tin or a tin alloy, historically a lead-antimony or tin-lead alloy, held between two metal end caps inside a glass tube. The glass is there so a failure is visible: the element melts, an arc forms, the tube fills with metal vapour and the arc is quenched as the pressure collapses, and the tube blackens.

facts.label: Element
facts.value: tin or tin-lead alloy, ~0.1-0.5 mm

facts.label: Voltage rating
facts.value: 250 V for the sizes used here

facts.label: Breaking capacity
facts.value: ~35-100 A for a small cartridge fuse

children.name: Ceramic wirewound fuse
children.description: A slow-acting fuse for the high inrush of the reservoir capacitor: a length of resistance wire wound on a ceramic bobbin, shunted by a strip of fusible alloy that runs beside it. The strip carries the current normally; the winding heats up when the fuse is overloaded and melts the strip, so the fuse tolerates a brief surge that would blow a straight element.

facts.label: Element
facts.value: resistance wire in parallel with a fusible alloy strip

facts.label: Characteristic
facts.value: time-delay (slow-blow); identified in the teardown by a small spiral inside the cartridge

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 A 250 V in the rectifier conductor of the 902503-02

children.note: The distinction between the two secondary fuses was made by inspection: the fast-acting one is a straight piece of fusible wire while the slow one contains a visible spiral or spring.

children.name: Thermal fuse
children.description: A one-shot temperature fuse: a fusible alloy link, often a fine wire of a low-melting alloy such as a bismuth-lead-tin-indium eutectic, bonded to the transformer or mounted in thermal contact with it. At its trip temperature - typically 100-130 C - the link melts and opens the circuit permanently. It cannot be reset, which is intentional: the fault that overheated the transformer is not allowed to be repeated.

facts.label: Trip temperature
facts.value: ~100-130 C typical

facts.label: Fusible alloy
facts.value: a low-melting eutectic, melting at a controlled temperature

facts.label: Fuse alloy
facts.value: often a small helical coil to make the melt more sensitive to a temperature ramp

children.note: The 13-83 teardown explicitly shows a thermal fuse between one end of the primary winding and the other line-in terminal.

children.name: X-rated line filter capacitor
children.description: A small polypropylene film capacitor connected across line and neutral to shunt radio-frequency noise that the switching action of the rectifier diodes and the regulator would otherwise inject back onto the supply. It is rated X - that is, for use between line and neutral - which in 1980s practice meant a recognised 250 V AC across-the-line capacitor with a defined failure mode.

facts.label: Voltage class
facts.value: X2 (rated for line-to-neutral) or X1

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: metallised polypropylene or metallised polyester

facts.label: Safety approval
facts.value: VDE, UL and CSA component recognition; the mark is printed on the body

children.note: Not established from a teardown photograph: that a specific Commodore brick contains an X-rated capacitor, although they are a standard fit in any listed appliance of this era and enthusiasts repairing original bricks commonly replace a RIFA suppression capacitor. The physics of the circuit requires it, but its presence in this specific assembly is inferred rather than documented. On the RIFA point specifically: RIFA was the dominant European supplier of X-rated metallised film capacitors in the 1980s, and parts from that era are now treated as a fire hazard in their own right - decades-old metallised-film suppression capacitors that have been sitting unused can draw leakage current, heat and in the worst cases short, which is why they are replaced on sight rather than tested. The failure was a design weakness, not a manufacturing defect.

children.name: Metallised polypropylene film capacitor
children.description: A 6-12 um polypropylene film is metallised with vapour-deposited aluminium to form the electrodes, then wound with a polypropylene or paper separator. Because the metallisation is only 20-50 nm thick it self-heals when a dielectric breakdown occurs: the arc evaporates the local metal, the arc is extinguished, and the damaged area is electrically isolated.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: polypropylene or polyester, ~6-12 um

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: vapour-deposited aluminium, ~20-50 nm

facts.label: Self-healing
facts.value: clears a dielectric fault by evaporating the electrode around it

children.note: Self-healing metallised film is why these capacitors are chosen for snubber and suppression duty: a transient across the line does not destroy the part.

roots.name: Commodore RF modulator module (VHF/UHF TV)
roots.description: The box on the C64 mainboard that turns the VIC-II's separate luma and colour outputs plus the SID's audio into one RF carrier for a television's antenna socket. Commodore published it as schematic 251025 and 251696: a handful of Japanese small-signal transistors, two miniature RF transformers, one trimmer capacitor and about thirty resistors and capacitors, with an RCA phono jack and a ten-way terminal strip on the edge of the board.

facts.label: US channel 3 (NTSC)
facts.value: picture carrier 61.25 MHz, chroma 64.25 MHz, sound 67.25 MHz, intercarrier 4.5 MHz

facts.label: US channel 4 (NTSC)
facts.value: picture carrier 67.25 MHz, chroma 70.25 MHz, sound 73.25 MHz, intercarrier 4.5 MHz

facts.label: UK channel 36 (PAL-I, UHF)
facts.value: vision carrier 591.25 MHz, chroma 585.75 MHz, sound 585.25 MHz, intercarrier 5.5 MHz

facts.label: Channel switching
facts.value: an H-L switch (channel 3/4) on NTSC machines; a tuning dial on PAL machines

facts.label: Output impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm, unbalanced

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: the C64's ~9 V unregulated rail, stabilised internally by a zener

facts.label: Terminals
facts.value: 1 +B, 2 sync+luma in, 3 colour in, 4 audio in, 5 composite out, 6 sync+luma out, 7 colour out, 8 intercarrier selector, 9 RF out, 10 channel trimmer

facts.label: Size
facts.value: ~63.6 x 62.6 x 24 mm for the 251025 module

roots.note: Three corrections to the identification. First, 55.25 and 62.25 MHz do not match any broadcast allocation: neither is US channel 3 nor a UK channel. US VHF channel 3 has its picture carrier at 61.25 MHz; the European PAL C64 shipped for UK channel 36, with the vision carrier at 591.25 MHz. Second, the part numbers 474040 and 474041 are not corroborated in any Commodore document; the documented modulator identifiers are the schematic numbers 251025 and 251696 and the part numbers 250469, 326130-01, 51A1-10 and the Mitsumi MD6 series. Third, the standard Commodore modules are discrete through-hole boards with Japanese transistors, not thin-film hybrids.

children.name: Video amplifier and clip network
children.description: Three small-signal transistors that take the VIC-II's pin 15 (sync + luminance) and pin 14 (colour), clip them with back-to-back diodes, and provide the two separate buffered outputs that go to the monitor connector as S-Video plus the summed composite that drives the RF section. Commodore called Q1-Q3 2SC1694 or equivalent; the earlier 251696 drawing uses 2SC2405.

facts.label: Q1, Q2, Q3 (251025)
facts.value: 2SC1694 or equivalent; Q4 2SC1730, Q5 2SC460, Q6 2SC2120

facts.label: Q1, Q2 (251696)
facts.value: 2SC2405 or equivalent; Q3, Q4 2SC2778; Q5 2SC2120Y

facts.label: Clamp diodes
facts.value: 1SS119 (251025) or MA151K (251696), back to back on the sync tips

facts.label: Typical network
facts.value: colour in via 68 nF with 1k/33k/43k bias and a 68 ohm emitter; luma in via 2.4 nF and 180 pF with 12k, 100 ohm and 400 ohm

children.name: 2SC1694 small-signal NPN
children.description: A TO-92 epoxy-potted silicon NPN with a 100-150 V collector rating, used as a common-emitter amplifier with a collector resistor and an unbypassed emitter resistor. The 2SC-prefix parts were the standard Japanese equivalents of the 2N series, and Commodore specified them as 'or equivalent'.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-92, epoxy-filled

children.note: Not established: the 2SC1694's 100-150 V collector rating and 50-150 mA class, the TO-92 epoxy-filled package, and Commodore's practice of specifying 2SC-prefix parts as "or equivalent" against 2N3904/2N4401. No datasheet for the 2SC1694 was consulted, so the ratings and package here are unsourced.

children.name: 1SS119 / MA151K clip diodes
children.description: Small-signal switching diodes, typically 50 mA class in a DO-35 glass can, wired back to back across the sync input. They conduct only on the tips of the sync pulses and the colour burst, which clips the signal to the amplitude a television's AGC expects and stops the modulator over-modulating.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: 1SS119 (251025) / MA151K (251696) or equivalent

facts.label: Package
facts.value: DO-35 glass, 2 mm diameter

children.note: Not established: the 1SS119 and MA151K designations, the ~0.6-0.7 V forward drop at 1 mA, the DO-35 2 mm package, and the back-to-back sync-clipping topology. The 1992 service manual confirms that the modulator takes the VIC-II's sync/luminance on pin 15 and colour on pin 14 and mixes them with audio, but says nothing about the clipping diodes. No datasheet for either part was consulted.

children.name: Picture carrier oscillator
children.description: A Clapp or Colpitts oscillator built around Q4 (2SC1730, a VHF transistor with an f_T above 300 MHz) and a miniature RF transformer, with a capacitive divider setting the feedback ratio. Composite video is injected into the oscillator's base network, so the video signal frequency-modulates the carrier directly: the modulation is done by varying the effective tank reactance with the video voltage, not by driving a separate modulator.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 61.25 MHz (NTSC ch 3), 67.25 MHz (NTSC ch 4), 591.25 MHz (PAL UK UHF ch 36)

facts.label: Feedback divider
facts.value: ~33.5 pF and 3.3 pF capacitors around the base

facts.label: Deviation
facts.value: +/-4.5 MHz from the carrier, i.e. +/-0.5 MHz of 5.5 MHz peak video

facts.label: Level network
facts.value: ~56 kOhm and 47 ohm series resistors with 30-51 pF capacitors

children.note: Channel setting is a resistor strapping and the channel trimmer, not a switched band. On NTSC machines an H-L switch on the rear panel changes a resistor or opens a contact in that network; on PAL machines there is a tuning dial instead, because the European sets have no fine channel selector - the dial is what makes a Commodore usable on a European television at all.

children.name: 2SC1730 / 2SC2778 VHF transistor
children.description: A VHF small-signal NPN in TO-92, chosen because its unity-gain bandwidth is several times the 60 MHz operating frequency so the oscillator starts easily and stays linear, and because its output capacitance is low enough not to detune the tank.

facts.label: f_T
facts.value: ~250-350 MHz class

children.note: Both are Japanese VHF small-signal types with f_T in the low hundreds of MHz; the exact figures are not verified against a 1982 data book.

children.name: Channel trimmer capacitor
children.description: The channel tuning element brought out to terminal 10 of the module: a small screw-adjusted trimmer in the 1-10 pF range, most often a ceramic plate or disc trimmer with a barium titanate or glass-ceramic dielectric, sometimes a stacked mica trimmer. It sits across the tank and is set once, at the television manufacturer's alignment step, against a sweep generator or a calibrated television signal. It is not one of the multilayer ceramic blocks that appeared later in the decade: a screw-accessible trimmer is what an alignment engineer needs, and a 1-10 pF part with internal electrodes would have been the wrong part for the job.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: ceramic screw-trimmer or mica trimmer, radial or dip

children.note: The 251025 drawing shows two adjustable trimmers in the RF area, one of which is the channel trimmer on terminal 10 and the other in the oscillator's feedback network. Later revisions replaced them with a fixed capacitor plus a resistor strapping for channel 3 or 4, which is why the channel switch exists at all.

children.name: MA57 tuning varactor diode
children.description: On the earlier 251696 drawing the tuning is done by D3, an MA57: a junction varactor whose capacitance falls as the reverse bias rises. Lifting the tuning out of the tank into a varactor keeps the temperature coefficient and the stray capacitance low. Later drawings use a mechanical trimmer in the same position.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: MA57 or equivalent (251696 note 2)

facts.label: Function
facts.value: variable reactance in the oscillator tank

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: a screw trimmer capacitor on terminal 10 in the 251025 drawing

children.note: A junction varactor in a 60 MHz television modulator is unusual - most designs tune with a trimmer - so the MA57 may be a varicap used for a small frequency-modulation or level function rather than for the channel. Its exact role in the 251696 drawing could not be confirmed from the scan.

children.name: Audio intercarrier path
children.description: A separate 4.5 MHz (NTSC) or 5.5 MHz (PAL) oscillator whose amplitude is modulated by the SID's audio output, then added to the picture carrier. Terminal 8 selects between the two: Commodore's drawing notes that terminal 8 shorted to ground is PAL and open is NTSC PAL/US.

facts.label: Intercarrier
facts.value: 4.5 MHz NTSC, 5.5 MHz PAL

facts.label: Input filter
facts.value: 22 uH choke and a ~10 nF capacitor

facts.label: Audio source
facts.value: the SID's amplified audio, fed from CN5 pin 3

children.note: Television sound is transmitted as FM on a subcarrier, and the tuner recovers it by beating the subcarrier against a local oscillator at the same frequency to produce the 6.0 or 5.5 MHz difference that every television's audio detector already handles. Using the standard intercarrier is why the modulator could be so simple - the set needed no second demodulator.

children.name: FM modulator network
children.description: The audio signal is fed to the intercarrier oscillator's base through a series resistor and a coupling capacitor, so the oscillator's amplitude follows the audio envelope. A varactor or a reactance modulator would be the higher-fidelity route; amplitude modulation is cheap and adequate because the television's own FM limiter removes most of the distortion.

facts.label: Series network
facts.value: ~2.2 kOhm and a ~10 nF coupling capacitor into the oscillator base

children.note: Modulation depth is kept low enough to avoid over-modulation and the characteristic buzz of a badly limited FM signal.

children.name: SID audio amplifier transistor
children.description: On the C64 mainboard the SID's pin 27 output is amplified by Q2 before it reaches CN5 pin 3 and the modulator; the modulator's audio input then loads that amplifier. The stage is a common-emitter NPN with a bias divider and an emitter resistor, running from the CAN +5 V rail.

facts.label: Device
facts.value: 2N3904 (Commodore stock 902658-01) in the mainboard audio path

children.note: This stage lives on the mainboard rather than inside the modulator, which is why the modulator's audio input could be a simple high-impedance network. The transistor itself is one of the C64's ordinary small-signal discretes (2N3904, Commodore stock 902658-01), from the same bins as the other board-level amplifiers, not one of the 2SC parts the modulator uses.

children.name: Intercarrier selector terminal
children.description: A single link or jumper on terminal 8 that reconfigures the intercarrier oscillator between 4.5 and 5.5 MHz. It is the PAL/NTSC configuration link for the whole module, and it is why one board could serve both markets with a single part change.

facts.label: Terminal 8
facts.value: shorted to ground = PAL (5.5 MHz); open = NTSC (4.5 MHz)

facts.label: Implementation
facts.value: a link or a switch contact in the oscillator bias network

children.note: Not established: terminal 8 being shorted to ground for PAL (5.5 MHz) and open for NTSC (4.5 MHz), and its implementation as a link or switch contact in the oscillator bias network. The 1992 service manual confirms two modulator variants exist - schematic 251025 for board 250425-01 and schematic 251696 for board 250407-04, the latter listed as "Modulator NTSC" - which supports the two-market point, but the terminal-8 strapping note is not in any source consulted.

children.name: RF output network and 75 ohm match
children.description: The picture carrier leaves the tank through a tap, is coupled out through a series capacitor, and is matched to the 75 ohm coax of the television's antenna input by a resistive network with a ferrite bead in the supply feed. Getting the match right is what stops the RF from reflecting back into the oscillator and pulling the carrier off channel as the television is tuned.

facts.label: Output impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm unbalanced

facts.label: Series match
facts.value: ~82 ohm and ~33 ohm resistors with a blocking capacitor

facts.label: Supply isolation
facts.value: a ferrite bead in the +B feed to the output stage

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: RCA phono jack, mounted on the module in the 251025 drawing

facts.label: Supply isolation bead
facts.value: a ferrite bead on the +B feed, 50-500 ohm at 100 MHz and near zero at DC

children.note: Most C64 installations put the phono jack on the rear panel of the machine and connect it to the modulator by a short coax or a twisted pair inside the case.

children.name: RCA phono socket
children.description: The US-style phono connector that carries the composite antenna signal. The centre pin is often nickel- or gold-plated brass and the outer shell is a turned brass or plated-steel barrel crimped into the body; the body is moulded in a glass-filled thermoplastic.

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: brass, nickel- or gold-plated, 0.8 mm centre pin

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm characteristic

facts.label: Body
facts.value: glass-filled nylon or polycarbonate

children.name: PAL UHF output stage
children.description: At 591 MHz a single transistor oscillator cannot drive a 75 ohm television input through a long lead, so the PAL modulators add a small tuned output stage and, in the later units, an output amplifier with its own bias network. The extra gain is what makes a PAL C64 usable on a European television without a booster.

facts.label: Gain
facts.value: a few dB of tuned amplification after the oscillator

facts.label: Matching
facts.value: tapped output coil plus a series blocking capacitor into the phono socket

children.note: No schematic for the PAL variant is available, so the topology here is inferred from the service manual's description of the PAL modules and from the general practice of UHF modulators of the period.

children.name: Modulator supply and zener stabiliser
children.description: The modulator runs from the C64's ~9 V unregulated DC rail - the same rail that feeds the cassette motor - not from the clean 5 V. Q6 (2SC2120) buffers the feed and a zener with electrolytics sets the working voltage for the analog sections.

facts.label: Input
facts.value: ~9-12 V DC from the C64's unreg 9 V rail, terminal 1 (+B)

facts.label: Zener
facts.value: ~8.2 V class (HZ-7A1 or equivalent in the 251696 drawing)

facts.label: Reservoir
facts.value: 220 uF and 100 uF electrolytics plus a 22 nF decoupling

children.note: Not established: that the modulator is fed from the 9 V unregulated rail, the 2SC2120 buffer, the ~8.2 V zener (HZ-7A1) and the 220 uF / 100 uF / 22 nF reservoir network. The 1992 service manual confirms the modulator exists as a numbered part (M1, Modulator 251696-01; Modulator NTSC 252405-01, on the 250407-04 board with modulator schematic 251696) and confirms the C64's supply rails, but its component-level supply network is not documented in the sources consulted.

children.name: 8.2 V Zener diode
children.description: A heavily doped PN junction reverse-biased into breakdown. The doping is so heavy that the depletion layer is only a few microns wide, which gives the device a very low capacitance and a fast, hard breakdown - ideal for a shunt regulator and for clamping.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: HZ-7A1 (~6.8-8.2 V) or equivalent

facts.label: Breakdown tolerance
facts.value: +/-5% for an ordinary zener

facts.label: Temperature drift
facts.value: ~+2 mV per volt of nominal per degree C

children.note: The C64 mainboard itself uses 2.7 V (1N4371) and 7.5 V (1N755) zeners in the cassette motor drive, so the same parts bins served the brick, the modulator and the mainboard.

children.name: Illustrative hybrid module construction (not Commodore)
children.description: ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY - this is not how any Commodore RF modulator was built. Both Commodore drawings that can be read (schematic 251025 and 251696) show a discrete through-hole board with Japanese small-signal transistors, two miniature RF transformers, a trimmer and about thirty resistors and capacitors, with an RCA phono jack on the module. What follows is the thin-film hybrid construction used by RF modulator modules from Japanese games manufacturers of the same period - a real and common alternative construction of the period, but no Commodore part number has been matched to it. Confidence in every node below is low as a statement about the C64 and high only as a statement about hybrid modules in general.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: 96% alumina or a hermetic ceramic; beryllia for the highest thermal conductivity

facts.label: Resistors
facts.value: thin-film or thick-film deposited and laser-trimmed on the substrate

facts.label: Encapsulant
facts.value: transparent or opaque epoxy, transfer moulded or dipped

facts.label: Leads
facts.value: gold- or nickel-plated DIP or castellated lead frame

children.note: Read this subtree as a comparison, not as a source. The observable Commodore evidence is the two schematics, both of which show a discrete board; the hybrid construction here is real technology of the period but its presence in a Commodore modulator is unverified and probably wrong for every documented part number.

children.name: Modulator part numbers and revisions
children.description: Commodore changed the modulator repeatedly and warned in the service manual that most modulators are different and the parts are not interchangeable between mainboards. Documented identifiers include 250469 (the short-board C64C), 326130-01, 51A1-10 Rev 2, and Japanese Mitsumi-built modules MD6-UE3603 for PAL and MD6-VA3402 / VA3403 / VA3405 for NTSC.

facts.value: 220 uF 16 V, 10 uF 16 V radial
2 x 4.7 uF 16 V radial

facts.label: Mitsumi MD6-UE3603
facts.value: 470 uF 10 V, 2 x 100 uF 16 V, 10 uF 16 V - the PAL version

facts.label: Mitsumi MD6-VA3402/3403/3405
facts.value: NTSC versions with different electrolytic sets

children.note: The part numbers 474040 and 474041 are not found in any Commodore document or parts list. If they are real they are most likely internal drawing or vendor numbers rather than the field-replaceable part numbers listed here.

children.name: Mitsumi-built modules
children.description: Mitsumi Electric was a major Japanese supplier of consumer-electronics subassemblies and shipped RF modulator modules to Commodore. The MD6 prefix denotes the module family; the suffix distinguishes NTSC from PAL and the electrolytic set.

facts.label: PAL
facts.value: MD6-UE3603

children.name: The 1984 C64C video path
children.description: The later C64 boards do not simply carry a better modulator - they changed where the signal is encoded. A dedicated video encoder IC generates the composite and separate luma/chroma outputs from the VIC-II's signals, so the video is encoded once, to a defined standard, outside the modulator; the RF modulator is then reduced to a device that only has to put that composite onto a carrier and add the audio. The contrast with the breadbin is that there the modulator itself was the video encoder as well as the modulator.

facts.label: Encoding point
facts.value: moved off the modulator onto a dedicated encoder IC

facts.label: Result
facts.value: composite and S-Video are available regardless of whether the RF modulator is fitted

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: the RF modulator becomes a purely analogue RF carrier generator

children.note: The existence of a dedicated CMOS video encoder on the C64C is well established in the enthusiast literature and C64-Wiki has a page stub for the part, but the device marking and its function in this context are not verified against a primary source. The US and PAL channel frequencies quoted above are standard broadcast allocations and are high confidence; the encoder part number is not.

children.name: The 'toad' module nickname
children.description: Early Commodore modulators are sometimes described by hobbyists as a toad or a blob: the epoxy-covered module sits on the mainboard with its lead frame splayed out, and from the top it does look like an animal. The nickname is not a Commodore part name - it exists only in the collector community.
children.note: No published source uses this nickname for the C64 modulator; it may come from a different platform. The attribution of the nickname to the C64 modulator is uncertain.

children.name: Why the RF picture was poor
children.description: The modulator is not the only reason the C64's television picture was soft and cross-talk-ridden, but it removes the last chance to recover quality: the VIC-II's own composite output already mixes luminance and chroma imperfectly, the television's 6 MHz vision channel is a narrow band-pass, the sound is on a separate subcarrier that leaks, and an analogue tuner adds its own noise. Every stage is lossy and they compound.

facts.label: Vision channel width
facts.value: ~5.5 MHz for a 625-line PAL signal in a 6 or 7 MHz slot

facts.label: Composite crosstalk
facts.value: the VIC-II's chroma is not properly band-limited before being added to luminance

facts.label: Set-side limit
facts.value: the analogue tuner's noise figure and AGC dominate at low signal levels

children.note: Empirical tests comparing the original modulator with modern replacements on the same CRT found almost no visible difference, which is the strongest evidence that the modulator was not the main limit - and on S-Video, bypassing the modulator's RF stage entirely, the original's luma and chroma outputs measured slightly better than most replacements.

children.name: Two composite paths in one module
children.description: Because the module has to keep working as a monitor passthrough, it carries two paths: the luma and colour signals are buffered straight through to CN5 so a monitor still gets an unmodified signal, while a separate summed composite is what drives the RF section. This is why S-Video from a breadbin is clean while the RF picture is not - the lossy parts of the chain are only on the RF path.

facts.label: Terminals 6 and 7
facts.value: sync+luma out and colour out, buffered from the inputs

facts.label: Terminal 5
facts.value: composite out, the sum, also fed to CN5 pin 4 on the 5-pin board

children.name: NTSC and PAL variants
children.description: The earlier 5-pin mainboard mixed sync, luminance and colour into composite on the board itself and fed that to the modulator, whereas the 8-pin boards pass luma and colour separately so the modulator can also provide S-Video. That difference is why the very first modulators are simpler than the later ones, and why the service manual says most modulators are not interchangeable.

facts.label: 5-pin board (326298-01)
facts.value: composite built on the mainboard; the modulator adds audio only

facts.label: 8-pin boards (250407-04, 250425, 250441-01, 250469)
facts.value: the modulator does the mixing and also passes luma and colour to CN5

children.note: Not established: that the 5-pin/8-pin split (composite on the mainboard versus luma-colour to the modulator) holds across all board revisions named, or that most modulators are not interchangeable for this reason; the board-number facts are as stated in the cited manual page.
