c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Polypropylene film
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: Made by polymerising propylene from a steam cracker in a slurry or gas-phase process; the resulting isotactic polypropylene is extruded into a thin film, biaxially oriented for tear strength, and wound onto a core. It is the normal dielectric for a suppression capacitor because it does not soften or shrink with temperature the way polyester does.

facts.label: Monomer
facts.value: propylene from the steam cracker

facts.label: Cracking conditions
facts.value: propylene from a steam cracker at 800-900 C and 0.5-2 s residence, then purified by selective hydrogenation and distillation

c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.name: Low-melting fusible alloy
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.description: An eutectic or near-eutectic mixture chosen so that it melts sharply at one temperature. A common mains fuse alloy is 50% tin, 50% lead melting at 180 C; a common thermal-fuse alloy is a bismuth-lead-tin-indium low-melting eutectic below 100 C. The alloy is cast or extruded into a strip or wire in air, then plated to keep it from oxidising.

facts.label: Example
facts.value: 50Sn/50Pb melts at 183 C; Bi-Pb-Sn-In systems melt at 70-120 C

facts.label: Sensitivity
facts.value: a thin section melts at a lower power because its surface-to-volume ratio is high

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Soda-lime tube glass
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: The fuse tube is a drawn borosilicate or soda-lime glass tube, chosen because it is dimensionally stable, easy to seal and does not outgas. Glass tubing is made by melting the batch and drawing the softened gather between rollers, so the wall thickness and diameter stay within a few microns along the length.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 70-74% SiO2, ~13% Na2O, ~10% CaO, with alumina and magnesia

c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler.name: Glass-reinforced switch body
c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler.description: Glass fibre is added to the switch body at 20-30% by weight and the compound is compression moulded. The glass reduces creepage and raises the distortion temperature, which is what keeps the moulding from softening near a hot transformer.

facts.label: Glass content
facts.value: 20-30% by weight, chopped 3-6 mm strands

facts.label: Distortion temperature
facts.value: ~150-200 C for a glass-filled phenolic

c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler.note: Not established: 20-30% glass content by weight in 3-6 mm strands, or the ~150-200 C distortion temperature. E-glass is documented as an alumino-borosilicate glass with less than 1% alkali oxides used for glass-reinforced plastics, and glass fibre reinforcement of nylon 66 is documented, but no source gives the glass fraction, the strand length or a distortion temperature for a glass-filled phenolic.

c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver.name: Copper and silver ores
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver.description: The moving and fixed blades are brass or phosphor bronze (copper with tin), and the contact faces are silver. Copper comes from sulphide concentrate and silver from argentiferous lead ores or from cyanide leaching of low-grade residues.

facts.label: Phosphor bronze
facts.value: ~90% Cu with 4-10% Sn, the standard spring carrier alloy

c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp.name: Metallised BOPP film
c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp.description: Biaxially oriented polypropylene film, stretched in both directions so the molecules line up to give high tensile strength and tear resistance in any direction, then vacuum-metallised with aluminium. The printing inks are solvent-based dyes and pigment pastes that are dried and overlaminated.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 20-40 um before metallisation

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: ~0.1 um of vapour-deposited aluminium

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.name: Aluminium anode foil
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.description: The anode is a 12-20 um aluminium foil that has been chemically etched in a hot chlorate or permanganate bath to roughen the surface into a high-area sponge. Because capacitance is proportional to real surface area, the etch multiplies the effective area by 30-100x and is the entire reason a 4700 uF part fits in a 25 mm can. The foil gauge, the rolling lubricant and the last work-hardening pass matter as much as the etch: at 12 um the metal is barely thicker than the oxide skin on it, so a single pinhole becomes a short. The stock foil and its rolling chain are the shared metal.aluminum.foil line, from the rolling ingot down to the slitter.

facts.label: Foil thickness
facts.value: 12-20 um for the anode; 6-9 um for the cathode

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: NaClO3/HCl or KMnO4 at 70-80 C for 10-60 min

facts.label: Surface gain
facts.value: 30-100x the geometrical area; pore size 0.5-2 um

facts.label: Route
facts.value: ingot -> hot roll 6 mm -> cold roll -> 12-20 um

facts.label: Lubricant
facts.value: kerosene or paraffin for the final pass

facts.label: Tensile strength at 12 um
facts.value: ~80-140 MPa, work-hardened

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.note: Mechanism documented, figures conflict. The 12-20 um anode gauge and the 30-100x surface gain are not corroborated and are contradicted by the best available source, which gives the anode foil as "~ 20-100 um made of aluminum with a high purity of at least 99.99%" and states that "the surface area can be increased by a factor of approximately 200 with respect to a smooth surface". The 0.5-2 um pore size, the NaClO3/HCl or KMnO4 etch at 70-80 C, the kerosene/paraffin lubricant and the 80-140 MPa tensile strength are not established.

c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte.name: Electrolytic electrolyte
c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte.description: An aqueous solution of an ammonium or amine salt - ammonium pentaborate was the classic low-voltage recipe - that forms the counter-electrode ion layer against the oxide. In an aluminium electrolytic the cathode reaction deposits a hydrated aluminium oxide or tin layer from the metal ion, and the leakage current is exactly that reaction rate.

facts.label: Typical system
facts.value: ammonium pentaborate / ammonium chloride, or an amine salt

facts.label: Leakage current
facts.value: I = kC V, roughly 2x the CV product rated current at 25 C

c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte.note: Partly contradicted. The documented low-voltage electrolyte systems are glycol/borax - "Electrolytes based on ethylene glycol and boric acid" - plus almost-anhydrous organic solvents (DMF, DMA, gamma-butyrolactone) and water-rich low-ESR systems; ammonium pentaborate as "the classic low-voltage recipe" is not among them, and the pH 4.5-7.0 range and the I = kCV leakage relation are not stated. What is documented is that the electrolyte supplies oxygen for self-healing, that service life is limited by electrolyte loss, and that organic-solvent systems give low leakage and long life.

c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.name: Cell separator
c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.description: A porous dielectric sheet between the anode and the cathode foil, keeping them apart without shorting. Low-voltage parts in 1980-82 used cellulose (paper) separators, which is the direct cause of the decades-later failure: paper is hygroscopic and absorbs electrolyte, and the carbonisation of that paper when leakage current rises shorts the cell.

facts.label: 1980-82 default
facts.value: cellulose kraft separator

facts.label: Later default
facts.value: polypropylene or polyethylene, and aluminium oxide-filled separators

c64.psu.transformer.pinboard.phenolic.name: Phenolic laminate board
c64.psu.transformer.pinboard.phenolic.description: Paper or cotton-linen web impregnated with phenol-formaldehyde resin under heat and pressure. Cheap, dimensionally stable and self-extinguishing, which is why it was the default material for transformer terminal boards and fuseholders.

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: phenol-formaldehyde, paper or cotton web

facts.label: UL flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB at typical resin content

facts.label: Phenol route
facts.value: phenol-formaldehyde at UL 94 HB, phenol from cumene hydroperoxide cleavage in the cumene/propylene-aromatics complex

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.name: Layer and interwinding insulation
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.description: Crepe paper or glass-cloth tape between winding layers, a wide kraft or composite tape wrap between the primary and the secondaries, and in the potted builds strips of polyimide (Kapton) film around the whole winding. The 1983-84 bricks visibly used masking tape on the core yoke edges and something like Kapton over the coil to keep the epoxy pour off the windings.

facts.label: Layer insulation
facts.value: crepe paper or muslin/glass cloth, ~0.2 mm

facts.label: Interwinding
facts.value: kraft-paper laminate or glass-cloth tape, 1-3 layers

facts.label: Creepage across windings
facts.value: 2-4 mm, set by the safety standard rather than by physics

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.name: Magnesium oxide sintering aid
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.description: A few tenths of a percent of magnesium oxide is added to 96% alumina before sintering to stop the ceramic over-shrinking and to fire it at a lower temperature, which is what makes 96% alumina affordable for a hybrid substrate.

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: sintering temperature down by ~100-150 C, shrinkage reduced

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.note: Not established: 0.2-0.5% magnesium oxide as a sintering aid, the ~100-150 C reduction in sintering temperature, and the resulting shrinkage control. The alumina article documents dense alpha-alumina ceramics and high-purity grades but does not mention magnesium oxide as an additive for 96% alumina, nor any sintering temperature.

c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.bismu.name: Bismuth and its ore
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.bismu.description: Bismuth is recovered commercially as a by-product of lead and copper refining, from anode slimes and from the residues of the Wohlwill process, and as a minor component of some tin and tungsten ores. Native bismuth and bismuthinite occur too, but refinery by-product is the industrial source.

facts.label: Content
facts.value: typically 0.01-0.1% of refinery residues

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Glass batch and silica sand
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: The batch is a few hundred kilograms of silica sand, soda ash, limestone and cullet melted in a regenerative furnace at 1400-1500 C. The silica sand, dug from high-silica deposits, is the leaf of the glass chain.

facts.label: Batch
facts.value: ~70% silica sand, ~15% soda ash, ~10% limestone, ~5% cullet

children.name: Regenerative furnace and cowper
children.description: A glass furnace cannot simply burn gas, because glassmelting needs far more heat than combustion can deliver at that temperature. The answer is regeneration: a Cowper regenerator beside the furnace stores the heat of the exhaust in a refractory mass, then blows the air through it on the next firing. The two 1980s designs were the regenerative box furnace and the unit-regenerator furnace.

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: natural gas or oil, preheated to 600-1000 C by the regenerator

facts.label: Waste-heat recovery
facts.value: ~20-40% of the fuel energy returned to the air blast

children.note: Not established: the Cowper regenerator beside a glass furnace, the 1400-1500 C working temperature, the 600-1000 C preheated air, or the 20-40% waste-heat recovery figure. No encyclopaedic source describes the regenerative box or unit-regenerator glass tank; the general principle that combustion cannot supply enough heat at glass-melting temperature is not itself in doubt, but nothing corroborates the figures.

c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.polypropylene.name: Polypropylene separator
c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.polypropylene.description: A microporous isotactic polypropylene film, 12-25 um thick and about 35-45% porous, made by extruding a film and stretching it or by solvent extraction so that the electrolyte fills the voids while the sheet still keeps the electrodes apart. It replaced paper because it absorbs no electrolyte and, when it overheats, softens instead of carbonising into a conductive bridge.

facts.label: Making the porous film
facts.value: extruded and stretched, or solvent-extracted; the monomer is propylene from a steam cracker at 800-900 C and 0.5-2 s residence

c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.polypropylene.note: Not established: the 12-25 um microporous isotactic polypropylene separator, the 35-45% porosity, and the stretch or solvent-extraction routes. The available source on aluminium electrolytics describes a paper spacer and does not mention a polypropylene separator; the claim that it replaced paper in service is likewise undocumented.

c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.cellulose.name: Cellulose paper separator
c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.cellulose.description: A thin kraft paper sheet made on a Fourdrinier or twin-wire machine from long-fibre softwood pulp cooked at 160-180 C in sodium hydroxide; the lignin is washed out into a black liquor that is burned for process heat, roughly 1.2-1.5 t per tonne of pulp, and the pulp is bleached with chlorine or hypochlorite before an acid wash. The paper absorbs electrolyte and swells, and on ageing it chars and shorts.

facts.label: Cooking
facts.value: 160-180 C in sodium hydroxide, 2-6 h

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: ~1.2-1.5 t black liquor per tonne of pulp, burned for process heat

facts.label: Bleaching
facts.value: chlorine or hypochlorite, then acid wash

facts.label: Sheet thickness
facts.value: 10-20 um kraft

c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.cellulose.note: Not established: the 160-180 C sodium-hydroxide cook, the 2-6 h cycle, the 1.2-1.5 t of black liquor per tonne of pulp, the chlorine or hypochlorite bleach and acid wash, and the 10-20 um sheet gauge. Kraft pulp being stronger than other pulps, darker, and bleachable, and sack kraft being made from softwood with high tear resistance, are documented; the capacitor-grade electrical paper specification and its manufacture are not.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.name: Crepe paper insulation
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.description: A lightly crinkled, unbleached kraft paper that stretches to follow the winding contour without bunching. Made on a Fourdrinier machine from a dilute suspension of long-fibre softwood pulp.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.g.name: Glass-cloth insulation tape
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.g.description: Woven E-glass yarn cloth, ~0.1 mm thick, silane-sized for adhesion, wound in the last layer before the outer tape. Glass has no moisture absorption and much higher dielectric strength than paper, which is why the safety-approved design puts it nearest the primary.

facts.label: Yarn
facts.value: E-glass (borosilicate, ~0.5-1.5% alkali), 204-136 tex

facts.label: Dielectric strength
facts.value: >10 kV/mm in the finished laminate

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.k.name: Polyimide (Kapton) film
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.k.description: A 12-25 um amber polyimide film used as the barrier between the coil and the epoxy pour and, in later builds, as the layer insulation. Its value is that it does not soften, dissolve or outgas in a hot epoxy cure.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.k.name: Pyromellitic dianhydride monomer
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.k.description: The diacid anhydride half of Kapton is made by air oxidation of pseudocumene to trimellitic acid and then dehydrating it - a petroleum-aromatics chain. The diamine half is 4,4'-oxydianiline or p-phenylenediamine, both aromatics intermediates.

facts.label: Diamine
facts.value: 4,4'-oxydianiline or p-phenylenediamine

facts.label: Polymerisation
facts.value: step-growth in dimethylacetamide at ~200-300 C

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.name: Mechanical wood pulp
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.description: Softwood (spruce/fir) is debarked, chipped, steamed and refined in a disc or refiner mill; the long fibres are ideal for electrical insulation paper because they give high dielectric strength and mechanical strength in the thin sheet.

facts.label: Mill water
facts.value: several tonnes per tonne of pulp, treated with alum, rosin and starch, clarified in a primary settling basin and recirculated

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.name: Softwood pulp
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.description: The species matters as much as the process: long-fibre softwood pulp from spruce, fir or pine gives the dielectric strength and tear resistance that electrical insulation paper needs, while hardwood pulp from birch or aspen gives opacity and printability and is used in the thinner papers. Softwood is bought as chips or as market pulp.

facts.label: Fibre length
facts.value: 2-4 mm for softwood, 1-2 mm for hardwood

facts.label: Electrical grade
facts.value: low-conductivity ash and low iron content are specified

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.note: Not established: the 2-4 mm softwood against 1-2 mm hardwood fibre lengths, the low-conductivity-ash and low-iron electrical grade specification, and the claim that hardwood pulp gives opacity and printability for the thinner papers. Softwood kraft for high-tear-resistance paper is documented; the electrical-grade specification and the species-to-property assignment are not.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.name: Magnesite ore
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.description: A magnesium carbonate rock mined in Austria, Spain, China and India, calcined at 1400-1700 C to magnesia. In the 1980s most ceramic-grade magnesia was calcined from seawater or from brine, but the rock remains the classic source.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: MgCO3, becoming MgO above ~1400 C

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.note: Not established: the Austria/Spain/China/India sourcing, the 1400-1700 C calcine, that seawater or brine was the dominant 1980s ceramic-grade source, or the silica input (silica contaminates cryptocrystalline magnesite as opal or chert; it is not a feed). The MgCO3 identity is as sourced.

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.perman.name: Potassium permanganate etchant
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.perman.description: An alkaline potassium permanganate bath oxidises the aluminium surface; the loose MnO2 sludge is removed by brushing or a nitric acid dip. The alternative chlorate chemistry was being phased out for safety and environmental reasons through the 1980s because chlorate/dioxide is toxic.

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: ~2-6% KMnO4 plus NaOH

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.perman.note: Not established: that an alkaline potassium permanganate bath at ~2-6% plus NaOH was used to etch capacitor foil, that the loose MnO2 sludge is brushed off or nitric-acid dipped, and that the chlorate route was being phased out through the 1980s. Potassium permanganate is documented as a strong oxidising agent and sodium chlorate's main commercial use as chlorine dioxide feed, but neither article mentions aluminium foil etching for capacitors.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.name: Impregnating varnish
c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.description: A low-viscosity, high-solids unsaturated polyester resin dissolved in styrene, with an organic peroxide cure catalyst. It cures by crosslinking rather than by solvent loss, so it shrinks very little and fills completely.

facts.label: Solids
facts.value: 60-70 wt% in styrene

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 150 C, 6-10 h; gel time minutes at 150 C

facts.label: Monomer
facts.value: styrene from benzene plus ethylene to ethylbenzene and then dehydrogenation; the varnish crosslinks rather than losing solvent

c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.note: Not established: 60-70 wt% solids in styrene, the 150 C / 6-10 h cure, the minutes-long gel time at 150 C, and the styrene-from-benzene-and-ethylene route. Vacuum impregnation of a completed winding with an insulating varnish is documented; the unsaturated-polyester-in-styrene formulation, its solids figure and its cure schedule are not.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel..name: Polyester-imide resin
c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel..description: The workhorse magnet-wire enamel of the 1980s. The base is a polycondensation of dimethyl terephthalate (or trimellitic anhydride) with polyols; the imide is introduced with a polyamide of trimellitic anhydride and a diamine such as ethylenediamine, which is what raises the class to H (180 C).

facts.label: Class
facts.value: H (180 C continuous)

facts.label: Key monomers
facts.value: trimellitic anhydride, terephthalic acid derivatives, diamines

facts.label: Route to the anhydride
facts.value: liquid-phase air oxidation of pseudocumene (1,2,4-trimethylbenzene) over cobalt/manganese acetate at 150-180 C, pseudocumene from catalytic reforming and aromatics extraction of petroleum naphtha

c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel..note: A coal-tar/cresol route to trimellitic anhydride existed and was used into the 1990s; the pseudocumene oxidation route became dominant in the 1980s, which is what makes this enamel a petroleum-aromatics product rather than a coal-tar one. The diamine half of the polyamide is ethylenediamine or a similar short-chain diamine, and it is the imide ring plus that diamine that lifts the insulation class to H.

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Film winding and vacuum metallisation
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: The film web is wound on a rotating vacuum-chamber drum while a wire feed head traverses it, laying down an aluminium layer 20-50 nm thick by resistive evaporation. At the same time a nucleation solution is dosed in to promote columnar crystal growth, so the metal grains follow the drum direction and the resulting capacitor has a low-loss, self-healing electrode. The web is slit to width and the capacitor is wound from slits onto a core.

facts.label: Evaporation rate
facts.value: ~1-3 nm per second, drum 300-800 mm diameter

facts.label: Slit width
facts.value: 5-30 mm for small parts

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.note: The un-metallised capacitor film is made on a separate line by a similar drum winder with a die and a chill roll; the metallising line normally sits downstream of the film line in the same plant.

children.name: Cast film production
children.description: Polypropylene is extruded through a flat die onto a chilled cast roll, then stretched and heat-set so it is strong in both directions, then slit into webs 20-60 um wide. A plain film is wound on the same type of machine as the metallised film, so the two steps are usually separate plants.

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: machine-direction orientation is typical for capacitor film

children.note: Not established: the cast-film route for capacitor film - extrusion through a flat die onto a chilled cast roll at 200-250 C, heat-setting, and slitting to 20-60 um webs - or the 20-40 um starting gauge. Polypropylene film is documented as extruded and, for biaxially oriented film, stretched in both directions; capacitor-grade machine-direction-oriented cast film on a chill roll is not documented.

c64.psu.potting.name: Epoxy potting pour
c64.psu.potting.description: From mid-1983 Commodore filled the case with a two-part epoxy so the whole assembly became one solid block: transformer, board, fuses, leads, the lot, in a minty-green or cool-grey mass. It made the unit tamper-proof and un-serviceable, and it turned out to be the primary cause of failure because the heat of the linear regulator could no longer escape.

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: minty green (3-83) or cool grey (13-83), both indicating different epoxy batches

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: the case is filled to within a few mm of the lid, leaving only the connector, cord and switch exposed

facts.label: Repairability
facts.value: effectively zero - extraction breaks the PCB and the transformer terminals

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: DGEBA (bisphenol A diglycidyl ether), epoxide value 0.52-0.57 mol/100 g

facts.label: Hardener
facts.value: triethylene tetramine (DETA) or an anhydride

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 24 h at 25 C or 2-4 h at 80 C

facts.label: Thermal conductivity
facts.value: 0.2-0.4 W/m.K unfilled; 1-3 W/m.K silica-filled

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: DGEBA (bisphenol A diglycidyl ether, epoxide value 0.52-0.57 mol/100 g) with triethylene tetramine or an anhydride hardener; 24 h at 25 C or 2-4 h at 80 C

c64.psu.potting.note: The epoxy is also an insulator thermally as well as electrically: it fills the natural convection paths around the heatsink and the transformer, so internal temperatures run 20-40 C above what the same parts see in an open case. Potting is a 1983-and-later build feature (both documented depotted units are 1983); the 1982 silver-label supply is reported as a vented repairable type with no epoxy pour, an adequate heatsink and a fused 5 V rail, but that rests on a single forum recollection and the changeover date is not established, so it is recorded here rather than modelled as a variant.

c64.psu.assembly.name: Brick assembly and final test
c64.psu.assembly.description: The order of operations is visible in the potted builds: the transformer is soldered to by the diodes and fuses at its own pins, the small board is populated, the LED and connector are fitted, the assembly is dropped into the case, epoxy is poured, the halves are screwed together, and the finished unit is then hi-pot tested, earth-continuity tested and burned in on load. Testing after potting is what lets a potted brick be safe and unrepairable at the same time.

facts.label: Order
facts.value: transformer wiring first, then board, then connector, then pot, then close and test

facts.label: Documents required
facts.value: the safety file: schematic, PCB artwork, BOM, transformer winding instruction, insulation system drawing, critical-components list and test instructions

facts.label: Earth continuity
facts.value: <= 0.1 ohm from the cord earth pin to the bonded point; in this all-plastic brick the earth stops at the transformer, so it is a continuity check on one bond

facts.label: Burn-in
facts.value: 2-8 h at rated load, 1.5 A on the 5 V rail plus up to 1 A on the 9 V AC winding, logging case temperature, output voltage and ripple

children.name: Hi-pot dielectric withstand test
children.description: 1-1.5 kV AC is applied between the primary and the joined secondaries for about one second, with the leakage current monitored and the test set tripping on either a flashover or an excess leakage current. It finds a pinhole in the enamel, a missing layer of insulation paper, or a solder splash bridging the bobbin.

facts.label: Trip current
facts.value: typically 5 mA for a basic-insulation product

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 50/60 Hz, or 0.1-0.5 Hz on modern electronic test sets

children.name: UL 478 / IEC 65 listing
children.description: The brick is certified as a component, not as a consumer appliance: UL 478 'Power Supply Units' in the United States, the equivalent IEC/EN 41003 and IEC 65 (BS 415 in the UK, VDE in West Germany) in Europe, plus CSA in Canada and Singapore's NLS scheme. Getting on the list required submitting the transformer winding instruction and the critical parts list, because those are the two things that cannot be verified by testing a finished unit.

facts.label: US standard
facts.value: UL 478, Power Supply Units

facts.label: File number seen
facts.value: 13J5, moulded into the case, with 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER'

facts.label: Other marks seen
facts.value: CSA, NLS (Singapore), and on European units VDE

children.note: UL 478 was the correct standard in 1982-84; it has since been withdrawn and replaced by UL 62368-1, which moved from a shock-hazard model to a hazard-based energy model. That change is why the old test voltages and limits quoted here no longer appear in current standards.

children.name: Isolation, creepage and clearance
children.description: The physical rules that make the layout safe: a primary-to-secondary creepage of about 6.4 mm and clearance of 3.2 mm for a 250 V basic insulation, the earthed foil between the windings, and the bobbin and terminal block designed so that a wire cannot fall across the isolation barrier. Every one of those dimensions is on the drawing and is checked at the follow-up inspection.

facts.label: Pinhole test
facts.value: a 0.5-1.0 mm hole in the earth screen is allowed to be probed without breakdown

children.note: Exact creepage and clearance figures depend on the pollution degree, the insulation type and the applicable standard edition; the values above are the order of magnitude for basic insulation at these voltages, not a substitute for the standard's tables.

c64.psu.assembly.note: Order confirmed in part: the 902503-02 teardown states that "The diodes and fuses are soldered directly to the transformer 'pins'" and that "The rest of the components are mounted on a small printed circuit board (PCB)". Not established: the epoxy potting and close-and-test sequence, because the same teardown states that this part number "is not 'potted' and can be opened and inspected" - potting applies to the later sealed bricks, not to the unit documented here. Also unestablished: the 2-8 h burn-in and the <= 0.1 ohm earth-continuity figure.

c64.psu.bulk-cap.winding.name: Winding and impregnating the cell
c64.psu.bulk-cap.winding.description: The anode foil (etched) and the cathode (bare aluminium foil, or the can itself in later types) are separated by the separator and wound on a mandrel into a compact roll, the leads are brought out, and the roll is impregnated under vacuum at 1-10 mbar with the electrolyte so the pores fill completely. Air left in the roll is the single biggest cause of high ESR. The can is then closed with a rubber bung pressed against the leads and a silicone or bitumen fill, and the leads are rolled down to set the dimensions.

facts.label: Vacuum impregnation
facts.value: ~1-10 mbar before electrolyte is admitted

facts.label: Squeeze
facts.value: rolled to expel electrolyte and set the dimensions

facts.label: Can seal
facts.value: rubber bung pressed against the leads, then a silicone or bitumen fill

c64.psu.bulk-cap.winding.note: Modern high-CV parts use a laser-drilled solid can as the cathode, eliminating the cathode foil and reducing ESR and inductance further.

c64.psu.heatsink.forming.name: Sheet folding and tapping
c64.psu.heatsink.forming.description: Strip or sheet is blanked, then folded on a press brake to a U; the mounting hole is punched or drilled and tapped with a thread-forming tap. Aluminium's low modulus means the fold must be given a generous inside radius or the sheet tears, and the tapped hole must be at least 1.5 diameters from the bend.

facts.label: Fold radius
facts.value: >=1.5 t inside radius

facts.label: Thread
facts.value: M3 or M4 roll-tapped (form tap) to avoid chipping the threads

c64.psu.heatsink.forming.note: Not established: the >= 1.5 t inside bend radius, the 1.5-diameter minimum distance from bend to tapped hole, and the M3/M4 roll-tapped thread. No encyclopaedic source covers press-brake bend-radius or thread-forming-tap practice; the general statements about aluminium's low modulus are common engineering knowledge but are not cited here.

c64.psu.regulator.mounting.name: Bolting the regulator to the heatsink
c64.psu.regulator.mounting.description: The regulator tab or TO-3 can is bolted to the folded aluminium plate with a thin layer of thermal compound - in 1982 typically a zinc-oxide paste in a silicone or hydrocarbon base, or sometimes simply a piece of thin copper foil. The thermal interface matters more than the compound brand: dry metal-to-metal contact is roughly ten times worse than a properly filled joint.

facts.label: Torque
facts.value: ~0.3-0.5 Nm on an M3 screw for a TO-3; overtightening cracks the can

facts.label: Interface
facts.value: 0.05-0.1 mm thermal grease, or a thin copper shim

facts.label: Isolator
facts.value: mica or silicone-rubber washer under a TO-3 collector tab

c64.psu.regulator.mounting.note: The 251053-02 teardown shows the heatsink as a 'featureless aluminium plate bent into a U-shape' with a drilled and tapped hole for the regulator screw; a drill bit slipped into the soft aluminium and had to be drilled out from several angles, which is a good illustration of how thin and soft the sink actually is.

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.name: Triple-diffused planar process
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.description: Three sequential dopings - collector-base, base-emitter, and a deep collector-emitter - through a photolithographically masked oxide. The heavy collector-emitter diffusion carries the load current while the shallow, tightly controlled base-emitter diffusion sets the gain and the breakdown voltage. This is the process that made 15 A transistors possible at all.

facts.label: Diffusions
facts.value: collector-base, base-emitter, collector-emitter (P, B, B, P)

facts.label: Base-emitter depth
facts.value: ~1-2 um; collector-emitter ~20-40 um

facts.label: Die
facts.value: typically 100 x 100 mm wafer, diced into 6 x 6 mm TO-3 dice

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.name: Die attach and hermetic TO-3 sealing
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.description: The die is brazed to the header in a hydrogen atmosphere at 700-800 C with an active-metal braze, or soldered with a 50Pb-50Sn or AuSn preform at 220-300 C; the header is then nickel-plated. The can is crimped or cold-welded onto the header with an annular glass or ceramic feedthrough insulator; mica or a thin mica-fibre washer goes between the can and the heatsink to isolate the collector while conducting heat.

facts.label: Brazing
facts.value: Ni-B or Au-Ag, 700-800 C, dry H2

facts.label: Feedthrough
facts.value: glass ring or BeO disc, 20-30 um seal gap

facts.label: Can
facts.value: nickel-plated low-carbon steel, cold-welded (soft solder) or crimped (hard solder)

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.name: Emitter wire bonds
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.description: Two to four 100-200 um aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the emitter metallisation to the emitter lead to carry the full emitter current; the collector current flows through the die's back contact straight into the header. Ultrasonic wedge bonding at 50-250 g per wire was the universal method - ball bonding was for fine-pitch.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 100-200 um aluminium, 99.99% Al + small Mg

facts.label: Force
facts.value: 50-250 g ultrasonic

facts.label: Bonds
facts.value: 2-4 in parallel on the emitter for a 15 A device

c64.psu.rectifier.diode.packaging.name: Die attach, wire bond and axial encapsulation
c64.psu.rectifier.diode.packaging.description: The die is die-attached to the anode lead with silver-loaded glass or a soft solder, one or two aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the cathode metallisation to the cathode lead, then the whole assembly is transfer-moulded or cast in an epoxy body filled with silicone gel to relieve the thermal cycle between the glass and the leads.

facts.label: Die attach
facts.value: silver-glass die attach at 430 C, or 80Au/20Sn solder reflow at 220 C

facts.label: Wire bond
facts.value: aluminium, 50-150 um diameter, ultrasonic wedge bond, 50-250 g

facts.label: Encapsulant
facts.value: epoxy or glass preform moulded at 150-175 C

c64.psu.rectifier.diode.packaging.note: Not established: silver-glass die attach at 430 C, the 80Au/20Sn reflow, the 50-150 um aluminium wedge bond, and epoxy or glass-preform encapsulation at 150-175 C for an axial rectifier. Wire bonding and epoxy as technologies are documented, but the specific attach, wire and moulding conditions for an axial diode have no source here.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.name: Layer winding on a coil winder
c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.description: A single-spindle or two-spindle coil winder turns the bobbin while traversing the wire, and the operator lays interleaved insulation between each layer with a slow-moving 'paper feeder'. Bobbin layers are counter-wound to flatten the coil, and the leads are brought out through the bobbin flange and dressed so they cannot chafe on the core.

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: single- or twin-spindle coil winding machine, 1500-4000 rpm

facts.label: Traverse
facts.value: cambered (offset) layers to give a level coil

facts.label: Tension
facts.value: ~50-150 g on 0.3 mm wire

children.name: Lead termination and crimped flag terminals
children.description: The winding leads are soldered or, in the 1983-84 bricks, soldered directly to the transformer's own pins; the line cord and interwinding conductors terminate in tin-plated brass crimp flags. Under the epoxy pour the crimps are the weak link - they can anneal and let go - and the PVC of the line cord is visibly browned right at the pin.

facts.label: Terminal
facts.value: tin-plated brass crimp flag or ring, ~6-8 mm2 wire

facts.label: Termination to transformer
facts.value: soldered to the bobbin-terminal pins on most builds

children.note: Crimping a soldered conductor into a screw terminal is explicitly discouraged by the repair community because the soft solder creeps and the joint goes high-resistance.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.note: Not established: single- or twin-spindle coil winding at 1500-4000 rpm, cambered offset layers, the ~50-150 g wire tension, and the paper feeder. No encyclopaedic source describes coil-winding machine practice or counter-wound bobbin layers; this is shop-floor process knowledge with no document behind it here.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.name: Polyester varnish impregnation and oven cure
c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.description: The finished assembly is vacuum impregnated with a thermosetting polyester or epoxy varnish so the winding becomes a solid block and cannot move at 50 Hz. Viscous impregnating varnishes were standard by the early 1980s; the alternative is dip-and-bake in an epoxy or a polyurethane.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: vacuum (30-50 mbar) then atmospheric impregnation

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: unsaturated polyester in styrene, or epoxy

c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.mould.name: Injection moulding the bobbin
c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.mould.description: Nylon is hygroscopic so the pellets are dried at 80 C for 4-8 h before moulding, then injection moulded at 240-280 C into a multi-cavity tool with hot runners and a mould temperature of 60-90 C. The mould cavity is polished because a flash of loose fibre on the winding slot would be a turn-coat defect.

facts.label: Drying
facts.value: 80 C, 4-8 h to <0.1% moisture

facts.label: Mould temperature
facts.value: 60-90 C, to crystallise the nylon

c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.mould.note: Not established: the 80 C / 4-8 h drying to below 0.1% moisture, the 240-280 C melt, the 60-90 C mould temperature, and the multi-cavity hot-runner tool. Nylon 66 is documented as being injection moulded and as needing to be kept dry because it absorbs moisture, but no source gives the drying schedule or the moulding window for a transformer bobbin.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.drawing.name: Wire drawing
c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.drawing.description: A 8 mm copper cathode rod or coil is pickled in sulphuric acid, washed, annealed in a continuous bright-annealing furnace at 500-700 C, then pulled through progressively finer dies with a phosphated soap lubricant. Ten or more die passes take 8 mm to 0.3 mm, and the die temperature is water-cooled to keep the copper from work-hardening to failure.

facts.label: Start
facts.value: 8 mm rod, ~99.99% copper

facts.label: Anneal
facts.value: 500-700 C continuous bright anneal, water-cooled

facts.label: Draw passes
facts.value: 10-15 dies for 8 mm to 0.3 mm

facts.label: Final tensile strength
facts.value: ~350-450 MPa for magnet wire

c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel.name: Polyester-imide enamel coating
c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel.description: The wire runs continuously through a die-casting oven where a 25-30% solids solution of the modified polyester-imide resin in cresol/xylene is applied, then through a 350-450 C curing oven, and through the same pair again for a second coat. The thermal cure crosslinks the resin to a hard film that resists varnish, oil and coolant.

facts.label: Coats
facts.value: 2 (Grade 2), 3 (Grade 3)

facts.label: Build
facts.value: 35-45 um for Grade 2 at 0.3 mm

facts.label: Cure oven
facts.value: 350-450 C, 20-40 s per coat

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.name: Punched E and I lamination
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.description: One E and one I punched from a strip of grain-oriented electrical steel by a high-speed progression press, roughly 200-600 strokes per minute. The die is a hardened tool-steel stamping die with a compound profile; the strip is fed on a roll and the interlamination burr left by the punch is small enough not to short adjacent plates.

facts.label: Press rate
facts.value: 200-600 strokes/min (high-speed progression press)

facts.label: Burr height
facts.value: ~10-25 um, sets the shorted-turn loss

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: the E is usually punched with the rolling direction across the yoke so flux runs along the grain

facts.label: Final thickness
facts.value: 0.35 mm (Hi-B) or 0.5 mm

facts.label: Silicon
facts.value: 2.0-3.5 wt%, added to kill eddy currents and raise resistivity

facts.label: Grain texture
facts.value: <100> grain, ~1 mm domain size

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: ~0.4-0.5 A/m after the magnetic anneal

children.name: High-speed stamping press
children.description: A vertical crank or hydraulic press with the compound E+I die in the lower ram and a blanking punch above. In a 1982-era plant the strip ran on a powered roll feed with a pilot pin for registration; the same press also cut the mounting-hole side features and the interleaving key.

children.name: Hardened tool-steel stamping die
children.description: Tungsten-chromium or high-chromium tool steel, hardened and ground, with the compound E and I outline in the same 25-40 mm stroke. Dies lasted millions of hits before the cutting edge rolled and the burr grew past the electrical-steel tolerance.
children.note: Not established: the tungsten-chromium or high-chromium grade, the 25-40 mm stroke, or the millions-of-hits die life for the 1982 lamination punch; no toolroom record backs this die.

Not established: the vertical crank or hydraulic press with a compound E+I die in the lower ram, the powered roll feed with pilot-pin registration, and the cutting of the interleaving key and side features in the same stroke. Electrical steel being "cut and converted into 'laminations'" is documented; the press, its feed and its die arrangement are not.

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.note: The steel itself is the shared metal.electrical-steel line: hot-rolled sheet from iron ore, cold rolling to 0.35 mm, a hydrogen magnetic anneal, and the aligned Goss texture. What is uncertain here is whether this brick used it. Oriented electrical steel was several times the price of hot-rolled mild plate and a 40 VA consumer transformer of 1982 could not justify it; the C64 Service Manual parts list calls for a laminated silicon-steel core without specifying an orientation. Treat the grade as unverified and the oxide-isolated stacking as the load-bearing detail.

c64.psu.transformer.core.stack.name: Core stack assembly and clamping
c64.psu.transformer.core.stack.description: E and I plates are stacked in alternating layers with the joints staggered so no section of the stack has an unbroken air gap, then clamped end to end by angle plates and bolts or by rivets through the yoke. The joints are the dominant core loss, so the assembler has to keep the interleaving sequence right by hand.

facts.label: Interleave
facts.value: E-I-E-I, joints staggered by half a pitch per layer

facts.label: Clamp
facts.value: steel angle plates and M4 bolts, or pop rivets

children.name: Clamp bolts and angle plates
children.description: Mild steel angle plates bolted across the yokes, or two long tie bolts through the core legs, with the axial clamp force chosen so the interlaminar pressure is roughly 3-10 kg/mm2 - enough to stop the stack buzzing at 50 Hz, not so much that the punched edges crack.
children.note: Not established: the 3-10 kg/mm2 interlaminar pressure figure and its units, or whether the C64 brick used angle plates or through-bolts; the buzzing-versus-cracking tradeoff is the stated design reason, not a measured value.

mb.rf-modulator.assembly.name: Modulator manufacture, alignment and test
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.description: A 1980s RF module was assembled by hand through a small number of components, soldered, then aligned: the channel trimmer is set against a television signal generator or a spectrum analyser, the intercarrier selector link is fitted for the market, the level network is checked on a video monitor, and the unit is burn-in tested with a television running.

facts.label: Soldering
facts.value: 60/40 tin-lead, wave or hand, flux residue cleaned

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: trim the channel capacitor to the exact vision carrier for the market

facts.label: Test
facts.value: modulate a known composite pattern and check picture, sound and intercarrier beat

facts.label: Solder and flux
facts.value: 60/40 tin-lead, 215 C liquidus (183-190 C at the 63/37 eutectic), rosin flux cleaned off with isopropanol or trichloroethane because rosin residue is hygroscopic and slightly conductive when damp

mb.rf-modulator.assembly.note: The 1980s practice was to align each module against a television set rather than a calibrated instrument, which explains why modules from different batches did not all land on exactly the same channel and why the rear-panel trimmer dial existed.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.name: Laser trimming of the film resistors
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.description: A laser is pulsed at a deposited resistor while a bridge measures its value, cutting a slot in the film a few microns wide to raise the resistance by a controlled amount. Each pulse changes the value by a known increment and the bridge closes the loop, so a resistor can be trimmed to 0.1% or better in a fraction of a second. Before laser trimming was cheap, the same slot was cut by abrading with a sand jet under a bridge, which was slower and only got to about 5%.

facts.label: Trim resolution
facts.value: ~0.01% per pulse

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.note: Laser trimming became standard in thick-film hybrid manufacture in the late 1980s; a 1982 module was trimmed by a mechanical probe that cut a slot in the film, or not trimmed at all.

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: Wafer processing and TO-92 moulding
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: The die is a small epitaxial NPN on a 100 mm P-type <111> wafer, sawn with a diamond blade, die-attached with a silver-glass preform, wire-bonded with 50 um aluminium and transfer-moulded in an epoxy-filled TO-92 tool at 150-175 C.

facts.label: Epitaxy
facts.value: 4-6 um N-type epi on a 10-20 ohm.cm P substrate

facts.label: Polycrystalline silicon
facts.value: 9N, grown by Siemens deposition from trichlorosilane at 1000-1150 C over DC-heated filaments, then pulled as a 100-150 mm Czochralski ingot and sawn to ~250-300 um wafers

facts.label: Mould compound
facts.value: black epoxy, usually silica-filled, transfer-moulded in a multi-cavity TO-92 tool at 150-175 C

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.note: This is one of about forty such transistors in a C64; the silicon branch of this tree carries the full wafer process.

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.name: Channel and region switching
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.description: Three different ways of reaching the right channel appear across the revisions. The US machines use a two-position H-L switch on the C64's own rear panel, wired to change a component value in the oscillator tank or level network; the switch is a low-voltage contact on the mainboard, not the brick's mains rocker. Some later units bring a variable capacitor or a trimmer out to a dial so the user can tune to their local station. PAL machines use the UHF band, so their oscillator runs at several times the frequency of the NTSC one and the tank, the output matching and an extra tuned output stage are different parts entirely.

facts.label: NTSC H-L switch
facts.value: switches between 61.25 and 67.25 MHz

facts.label: PAL dial
facts.value: continuous tuning around 591.25 MHz (UK channel 36)

facts.label: Implication
facts.value: one modulator part number could not serve both markets, which is why the service manual lists several

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.note: The C64 Wiki notes that beside the RF jack you often see an H-L switch for channels 3 and 4 (NTSC only) or a control dial for adjusting the oscillator frequency - the two mechanisms correspond to the two markets.

c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..name: Silver refining from lead residues
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..description: Argentiferous lead concentrates are roasted and smelted, and the silver reports to the lead bullion, from which it is recovered by Parkes' process: the bullion is cooled so copper crystallises out and is skimmed, then zinc is added, which scavenges the silver and gold into a zinc crust that is skimmed off and distilled. The crude silver is cupelled and electrolytically refined to 99.9% or better.

facts.label: Parkes process
facts.value: zinc added at 1-2% of the bullion mass, crust skimmed at 600-700 C

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: Moebius or Balbach-Thum electrolysis, silver nitrate electrolyte

c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..note: Silver for electrical contacts has always been by-product metal, so its price is set by the lead and zinc smelters rather than by silver mines; most of the 1982 supply came from Mexico, Peru and the Soviet bloc.

children.name: Cupellation
children.description: An ancient refining step that survives into the 1980s for precious metals: the metal is melted with a lead oxide flux and blown with air, which oxidises the lead and the base metals to litharge that floats off, while the silver and gold stay as metal. Agricola described it in the 16th century and it is still the standard way to remove base metal from silver dross.

facts.label: Litharge
facts.value: PbO, the oxidised lead, absorbed into the bone ash cupel

c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp..name: Biaxial orientation
c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp..description: A cast polypropylene or cast polyethylene film is stretched in the machine direction, cooled, then stretched again in the transverse direction and heat-set. The two stretching steps line the polymer chains up in both directions, so the film has high tensile strength and tear resistance whatever the pull direction - which is exactly why a torn BOPP label ends in a straight line rather than a ragged one.

facts.label: Stretch ratios
facts.value: ~3-5x machine direction, ~4-10x transverse for a label film

facts.label: Set temperature
facts.value: 110-140 C to freeze the orientation

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.name: Chemical etching of the anode foil
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.description: The foil is threaded continuously through an etch tank at 70-80 C. Sodium chlorate with hydrochloric acid, or potassium permanganate, dissolves aluminium faster where the surface is already rough, so the etch runs away into a deep microscopic pore structure rather than eating away uniformly. The etched foil is rinsed, dried and cut to length.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: NaClO3 + HCl, or KMnO4 in an alkaline bath

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 10-60 min depending on the required pore depth

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.note: Not established: sodium chlorate with hydrochloric acid or potassium permanganate as the etchant, the 70-80 C tank temperature, the 10-60 min dwell, and the runaway-into-pore-structure mechanism. What is documented is generic: the anode is "etched (roughened) in an electrochemical process to increase the effective electrode surface". The specific etch chemistry and its process conditions have no source here.

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.formation.name: Electrolytic formation of the anode oxide
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.formation.description: The wound wet cell is energised from a DC source at a voltage ramped up to the rated working voltage. At the anode the aluminium oxidises to a dense amorphous alumina film only a few nanometres thick - the dielectric. Raising the voltage thickens the film; raising the temperature thickens it faster but also lets it dissolve, which is why forming is done hot and forming voltage is always lower than the operating voltage.

facts.label: Forming voltage
facts.value: ~1.1-1.3x the rated voltage, ramped over 1-4 h

facts.label: Film thickness
facts.value: 2-5 nm of amorphous Al2O3 at 16 V rating

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~8-10 for amorphous alumina

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.formation.note: Mechanism documented, figures conflict. Documented: dielectric thickness is proportional to forming voltage, and "due to standardized safety margins the actual forming voltage of electrolytic capacitors is higher than the rated voltage of the component"; amorphous oxide has "a dielectric ratio of ~ 1.4 nm/V". That gives roughly 14 nm at a 10 V rating, not the 2-5 nm claimed here at 16 V. Not established: the 1.1-1.3x ramp, the 1-4 h ramp time, the 80-95 C formation temperature and the ~8-10 dielectric constant.

mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.name: Video encoder integrated circuit
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.description: A mask-programmed device that takes the VIC-II's luminance and chrominance plus the synchronisation inputs and generates composite video and separate luma and chrominance outputs internally, using on-chip resistor-string DACs for the levels. Building the encoder alongside the VIC-II was what made the S-Video output clean enough to be worth using.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: luminance/chrominance to composite and S-Video encoding, with internal level DACs

facts.label: Clock
facts.value: driven from the 14.318 MHz colour clock

mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.note: The exact part number and its manufacturer are not verified against a primary source; this is a description of the function rather than of a confirmed device.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.name: Alumina substrate and its ceramic processing
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.description: A thin, smooth, thermally conductive ceramic sheet. Alumina is made by calcining purified aluminium hydroxide, pressing or tape-casting it with an organic binder, sintering at 1500-1700 C, then lapping and laser-cutting the finished sheets to thickness. It is inert, dimensionally stable and easy to metallise.

facts.label: Alumina content
facts.value: 96% standard, 99.5% high-purity

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.25-1.0 mm, lapped and polished

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.name: Thin-film and thick-film resistor networks
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.description: A film of nickel-chromium is deposited by vacuum evaporation or sputtering onto the alumina, then patterned by photolithography and etching. Because the sheet resistance of the film is very uniform the as-deposited value is already within a few percent, so a trim brings it to its exact value.

facts.label: Thin film
facts.value: NiCr sputtered, ~50-500 ohm per square

facts.label: Trim
facts.value: sand-blast trim to 5-10% before laser trimming; laser trim to 0.1-1% became cheap only in the late 1980s

facts.label: TCR
facts.value: 25-100 ppm/K, far better than a thick-film resistor

facts.label: Thick film
facts.value: screen-printed ruthenium-oxide cermet, 10-1000 ohm per square, fired at 800-900 C for 10-30 min; the glass frit content sets the resistance

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.note: Thick film, a screen-printed ruthenium-oxide paste fired at 800-900 C, was the normal choice for a cheap RF module in 1982; thin film was reserved for precision timing and gain stages.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.epoxy-enca.name: Epoxy encapsulant as RF seal
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.epoxy-enca.description: A clear or opaque filled epoxy poured or transfer moulded over the finished substrate. In RF modules it does three jobs at once: it excludes moisture and contaminants, it holds the components against vibration, and - because it is a low-loss dielectric with a stable dielectric constant - it fixes the stray capacitance around the tank, which is what stops the carrier drifting with humidity. A conductive epoxy variant is used as a ground plane on the reverse of the substrate.

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: silica or alumina flour at 40-70% by weight for low CTE and low moisture uptake

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~3.5-4.5, low and stable

facts.label: CTE
facts.value: 15-25 ppm/K filled, versus 50-70 unfilled

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.epoxy-enca.note: Not established: silica or alumina flour at 40-70% by weight, a 3.5-4.5 dielectric constant, the 15-25 ppm/K filled against 50-70 unfilled CTE, and the specific RF role of fixing stray capacitance around the tank. Epoxy as a thermosetting encapsulant is documented; the filler loading, the electrical figures and the RF rationale are not.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.name: Gold-plated DIP lead frame
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.description: The substrate is attached to a lead frame by reflow or conductive epoxy, and the frame's pins are plated. Gold is used where the RF signal leaves the module, because a nickel or tin surface has poor conductivity at 60 MHz and tarnishes; in cheap modules only the signal pins are gold and the supply pins are tinned.

facts.label: Frame
facts.value: nickel-iron or copper alloy strip, stamped and formed

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: gold over nickel on signal pins, tin on supply pins

facts.label: Gold thickness
facts.value: ~0.5-2 um hard gold in the 1980s

facts.label: Plating thickness
facts.value: about 0.5-2 um of hard gold over nickel on the signal pins, tin on the supply pins

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.note: Hard gold plating came in because gold on soft gold diffused into the bond pads.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.name: Hybrid module assembly and transfer moulding
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.description: The die or chip components are bonded to the substrate, the lead frame is attached, and the whole assembly is transfer moulded in epoxy: a silicone-rubber mould loaded with epoxy powder is vibrated to pack it around the part, the encapsulant is pressed in, and it is cured at 150-175 C. This is the same process used for every integrated circuit in the machine.

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 20-60 s per shot for a small mould

facts.label: Curing
facts.value: 150-175 C, several minutes

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.note: For a hybrid the mould is room-temperature or low-temperature cured so that the deposited film and any surface-mounted parts survive; for an IC the epoxy is moulded at full cure temperature.

children.name: Attaching the substrate to the lead frame
children.description: The substrate is aligned to the lead frame to within a few microns, given a thin coat of conductive epoxy - silver-filled epoxy is the usual choice because it cures at only 150-200 C - or a screen-printed solder paste is printed and reflowed, then the assembly is baked so the die attaches without stress. Silver-filled epoxy has no metallurgical bond and can debond with thermal cycling, which is the classic failure mode of a hybrid module.

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: 5-25 um for conductive epoxy; 1-10 um for solder attach

facts.label: Curing
facts.value: 150-200 C for 1-4 h for silver epoxy

children.note: Not established: the 5-25 um conductive-epoxy and 1-10 um solder alignment figures, the 150-200 C / 1-4 h silver-epoxy cure, and the claim that silver-filled epoxy has no metallurgical bond and debonds on thermal cycling. No source consulted covers hybrid-module substrate-to-lead-frame attachment.

children.name: Silver-filled conductive epoxy
children.description: Epoxy resin loaded with 50-80% silver flakes. The flakes touch each other to form a percolating conductor while the epoxy gives mechanical strength and cures at a temperature the chip and substrate tolerate. Bulk resistivity is about 0.001-0.01 ohm.cm, two to three orders of magnitude worse than a metal, so it is used for bonding and for conductive fill, never for signal.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 50-80 wt% silver flake, ~5-50 um flakes

children.note: Not established: 50-80 wt% silver flake loading, ~5-50 um flakes, and the 0.001-0.01 ohm.cm bulk resistivity, and the gold-filled non-migrating alternative at roughly ten times the cost. Epoxy resins as a family are documented; silver-filled conductive epoxy as a specific composition and its resistivity are not.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.name: Chip inductor and chip capacitor
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.description: In a hybrid RF module the high-value capacitors and the low-value inductors are not screen-printed but chip-bonded: a fired ceramic chip capacitor with metallised terminations is reflowed onto the substrate, and an inductor is a tiny spiral of metallised polyimide on a ceramic chip. The polyimide is photosensitised, plated, etched and diced, so the inductance is set by the artwork rather than by a winding machine.

facts.label: Chip capacitor
facts.value: fired BaTiO3 or tantalum, terminated in fired silver or a solderable metal

facts.label: Chip inductor
facts.value: photosensitised polyimide spiral on alumina, 1-100 nH typical

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.note: Chip inductors were a 1990s development for RF modules above about 100 MHz; a 60 MHz television modulator in 1982 used a wound coil, and the chip parts that were used were almost all capacitors.

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment.name: Substrate alignment and RF screening
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment.description: After assembly the module is screened: an RF sweep is injected at the output terminal and the response curve is checked against a mask. A damaged substrate, a lifted chip termination or a cracked lead frame shows up as a notch in the response, which is why a hybrid modulator's yield is dominated by the ceramic and the assembly rather than by the design.

facts.label: Test method
facts.value: swept-response substitution with an RF sweep generator and a detector

facts.label: Pass criterion
facts.value: within a mask on insertion loss, return loss and resonance

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment.note: Screen-on-substrate testing in the bare form was a 1990s technique; a 1982 hybrid was tested only after encapsulation, so a realignment meant re-encapsulating.

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Refractory lining and checker plates
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: The furnace and regenerator are lined with refractory brick, and the regenerator's internal mass is a stack of checker plates of silica or chrome-magnesite. Refractory brick is made by pressing or hand-moulding a graded mineral aggregate with a clay binder and firing it in a tunnel or car kiln; the grading, not the chemistry, is what gives a lining its thermal-shock resistance.

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1400-1500 C for silica brick; 1600-1750 C for magnesia

facts.label: Silica brick
facts.value: ~94-98% SiO2, use limited to about 1500 C

facts.label: Magnesia brick
facts.value: 85-95% MgO, used to ~1700 C

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.note: Beryllium oxide had even higher conductivity but was withdrawn from general use in the 1980s because of its toxicity.

c64.mains.earthing.name: Protective earth bonding
c64.mains.earthing.description: The brick is entirely moulded ABS with no metal chassis, so there is nothing external to bond earth to. The earth conductor runs from the plug, into the epoxy-filled case, and terminates on the aluminium or copper screen buried between the transformer's primary and secondary windings. The earthing path therefore closes and opens entirely inside one potted block, and the C64 itself has an unconnected earth: the supply behaves like a Class II appliance even though it carries an earth conductor.

facts.label: Case
facts.value: all-plastic ABS, no metal enclosure

facts.label: Bond point
facts.value: the interwinding screen inside the transformer

facts.label: Continuity test
facts.value: <= 0.1 ohm from the cord earth pin to the bonded screen

c64.mains.earthing.note: A two-conductor cord with no earth at all would have been perfectly acceptable for a doubly-insulated Class II appliance of this size, and some Commodore builds do use a two-wire cord. Carrying an earth into an all-plastic supply is belt-and-braces: it protects against the earth pin being energised by a primary-secondary fault inside the transformer, which is precisely what the interwinding screen does.

c64.mains.approvals.name: Safety approvals and standards
c64.mains.approvals.description: The brick is certified as a component rather than as an appliance. In the United States that is UL 478, Power Supply Units, with the file number moulded into the case - 13J5 with 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER' on the 3-83 build. In Canada it is CSA, in Singapore the NLS scheme, and in West Germany VDE. Each is a recognised component mark; the finished C64 was then certified separately under whichever national scheme applied to the appliance.

facts.label: US
facts.value: UL 478, file 13J5

facts.label: Canada
facts.value: CSA

facts.label: Singapore
facts.value: NLS

facts.label: Europe
facts.value: VDE; the appliance-level standard was IEC 65 / BS 415 / EN 41003

c64.mains.approvals.note: UL 478 was the correct US standard in 1982-84 and has since been withdrawn in favour of UL 62368-1, which replaced the shock-hazard model with a hazard-based energy model; the test voltages and limits quoted in this tree are the 1980s values and will not appear in the current standard.

children.name: The safety file
children.description: Listing is not just a test. The applicant submits a design file: schematic, printed-board artwork, bill of materials, critical-components list, the transformer's winding instruction and insulation system drawing, the enclosure material specifications, and the test report. The follow-up inspection checks that production still matches the file, and it is the reason a safe transformer cannot simply be substituted with a cheaper one after manufacture.

facts.label: Critical parts
facts.value: the transformer, the line capacitor, the switch, the fuse holder, the cord set and the enclosure flammability

facts.label: Follow-up
facts.value: periodic factory inspection of the listed factory

facts.label: Relationship to the listing
facts.value: the design file is what the applicant submits to obtain the listing; the brick's own final-test branch carries the type tests themselves

children.note: Not established: the contents of the design file submitted for this supply - schematic, PCB artwork, BOM, transformer winding instruction and insulation-system drawing, enclosure material specification - and the periodic follow-up factory inspection that checks production still matches. UL is documented as certifying products against its own standards; the file-and-follow-up regime is not documented in the sources consulted.

children.name: Routine production tests
children.description: Beyond the type tests, every unit gets a dielectric withstand test between the primary and the secondaries, an earth-continuity test, and a functional test with a load on both outputs. The dielectric withstand is the test that actually keeps people alive, because the failure it detects - a foil short, a pinched wire, a solder splash across the bobbin - is the fault that puts mains on a 5 V rail.

facts.label: Dielectric withstand
facts.value: 1500-2500 V AC for about 1 s, leakage current monitored

facts.label: Functional
facts.value: both outputs loaded and measured, case temperature observed

facts.label: Where the dielectric withstand lives
facts.value: the brick's own assembly branch carries the hi-pot, earth-continuity and burn-in tests; this node is the standards view of the same three

children.name: Lot sampling and the critical-component control plan
children.description: Listing does not mean every unit is tested at every test. Instead the manufacturer submits a control plan: the dielectric withstand and earth continuity are 100% tests because they are the safety-critical ones, while the routine functional and leakage-current checks are sampled at an agreed quality level - typically one in three to one in thirty, with any failure escalating the lot to 100%. Critical components (the transformer, the switch, the fuse, the line capacitor, the cord set) come only from named manufacturers and are subject to incoming inspection.

facts.label: Safety tests
facts.value: 100% dielectric withstand, 100% earth continuity

facts.label: Functional tests
facts.value: sampled, typically AQL 2.5 or 6.5

facts.label: Critical parts
facts.value: from a named-vendor list only, with certificate-of-conformance required

facts.label: Lot size
facts.value: typically one shift, one line, one component lot

facts.label: Reject number
facts.value: from the original sample plan, not re-derived

children.note: The AQL concept and the critical/major/minor defect split are standard (ANSI/ASQ Z1.4), but not established: this control plan. No document states that dielectric withstand and earth continuity were 100% tests while functional and leakage were sampled, nor the AQL 2.5 or 6.5 levels, nor that critical parts came from a named-vendor list with certificate of conformance.

Not established: that this specific three-test set (dielectric withstand, earth continuity, loaded functional test) was applied to every unit of this supply, or the 1500-2500 V / 1 s withstand level, the <= 0.1 ohm earth-continuity limit, or the burn-in loading. The dielectric withstand test itself is a documented production test; its levels are set by the applicable product standard, not stated here.
